{kb}/新论文/2026-10-24/Scalpel-SAM_A_Semi-S.text: Scalpel-SAM: A Semi-Supervised Paradigm for Adapting SAM to Infrared Small Object Detection Zihan Liu∗, Xiangning Ren†, Dezhang Kong‡, Yipeng Zhang§, and Meng Han‡ ∗School of Computer Science, Chengdu University, Chengdu, 610106, China †China University of Geosciences, Beijing, China ‡Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China §Intelligent Computing Infrastructure Innovation Center, Zhejiang Lab, Hangzhou, China Abstract—Infrared small object detection urgently requires semi-supervised paradigms due to the high cost of annotation. However, existing methods like SAM face significant challenges of domain gaps, inability of encoding physical priors, and inherent architectural complexity. To address this, we designed a Hierarchical MoE Adapter consisting of four white-box neural operators. Building upon this core component, we propose a two-stage paradigm for knowledge distillation and transfer: (1) Prior-Guided Knowledge Distillation, where we use our MoE adapter and 10% of available fully supervised data to distill SAM into an expert teacher (Scalpel-SAM); and (2) Deployment- Oriented Knowledge Transfer, where we use Scalpel-SAM to generate pseudo labels for training lightweight and efficient downstream models. Experiments demonstrate that with minimal annotations, our paradigm enables downstream models to achieve performance comparable to, or even surpassing, their fully supervised counterparts. To our knowledge, this is the first semi-supervised paradigm that systematically addresses the data scarcity issue in IR-SOT using SAM as the teacher model. Index Terms—Semi-Supervised Learning, Infrared Small Ob- ject Detection, Segment Anything Model I. INTRODUCTION Infrared small object detection (IR-SOT) serves as a founda- tional technology in defense security, disaster rescue, and other critical areas, owing to its unique capability to identify thermal signatures under all-weather conditions and in total darkness where visible light systems fail [1], [2]. However, IR-SOT is being plagued by two major bottlenecks: First, infrared images have extremely minute targets, low signal-to-noise ratios, and a severe lack of textural cues and color cues that are abundant in natural images[1]. Second, obtaining pixel-level ground truth annotations incurs an exceedingly high cost [2]. The laborious and challenging process of manual labeling makes traditional methods, which rely on large-scale supervision, impractical. As such, exploring how to achieve efficient detection in the face of scarce data has become an urgent demand in this field. Large foundation models, exemplified by Segment Anything Model (SAM)[3], offer a solution to this impasse. This is because SAM’s unique prompt-driven architecture can han- dle minimal, sparse guidance and output high-quality, dense segmentation masks. However, SAM was not designed for the specific physical properties of IR-SOT. Therefore, when we attempt to directly apply it to this specialized task, there are three challenges that must be addressed: (1) severe perfor- mance failure due to the domain gap, as visually demonstrated Stage One: Knowledge Distillation Based on Hierarchical MoE Adapter Labeled Data SAM Hierarchical MoE Adapter Supervised Learning Generate Pseudo Labels Unlabeled Data Stage Two: Knowledge Transfer for Lightweight Deployment Pseudo Labels Unlabeled Data Backpropagation Loss Calculation Segmentation Result Pseudo Labels The final lightweight, efficient, and prompt-free downstream model (a) (b) Fig. 1: The proposed paradigm and the visual evidence of the challenge. To systematically address these three challenges, we pro- pose a two-stage knowledge distillation and transfer paradigm, as shown in Figure 1a. The Stage One addresses challenges 1 and 2, where we design an innovative Hierarchical MoE Adapter to fine-tune SAM into an expert teacher called Scalpel-SAM. Its core is an expert toolkit composed of four white-box neural operators (Physics-Informed Manifold Dif- fusion Operator (PIMDO), Spectral Prism Decoupler (SPD), Hyper-Parameterized Local Statistics Modulator (HPLSM), Topology-Guided Deformable Sampler (TGDS)). These oper- arXiv:2512.22483v1 [cs.CV] 27 Dec 2025 ators explicitly encode anisotropic diffusion, frequency decou- pling, local statistical adaptation, and topological connectivity priors into the network structure, elevating PEFT from a generic black-box into an interpretable regulator with surgical precision. The Stage Two tackles challenge 3, where we use the expert teacher trained in the first stage and generate high-quality pseudo labels. This pivotal step both amplifies the knowledge learned from the 10% supervised data and enables the knowledge to be transferred to a lightweight, efficient, and prompt-free student model, thereby drastically reducing the final deployment cost. This paradigm successfully transfers SAM’s powerful prior knowledge into a deployable lightweight model while solving the dual dilemmas of model capability and data costs. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of our paradigm. The results demonstrate that by applying our paradigm, the performance of downstream models approaches or even surpasses that of their fully supervised counterparts. To our knowledge, no prior semi-supervised paradigm in IR-SOT has managed to close this performance gap, let alone exceed the fully supervised upper bound. We also publish our code on https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ Scalpel-SAM(Anonymized for review). The contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: • We propose a two-stage knowledge distillation and trans- fer paradigm, which can automatically label vast data and help train downstream models. To our knowledge, this is the first semi-supervised learning paradigm for IR-SOT detection. • We design a Hierarchical MoE Adapter that replaces the generic black-box structure of traditional PEFT methods with a domain-principle-driven expert toolkit, which can mimic a human expert’s progressive thought chain for target analysis and elevate PEFT into a domain-driven, highly interpretable adaptive regulator. • Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our paradigm approaches or even surpasses fully supervised performance using only 10% of the labeled data. II. METHODOLOGY For clarity, all mathematical symbols and notations used in our methodology are shown in Table I. A. Overview: Knowledge Distillation and Transfer Paradigm Our paradigm decouples the complex adaptation and learn- ing process into two distinct stages. 1) Stage One: Knowledge Distillation Based on Hierar- chical MoE Adapter: The goal of this stage is to utilize a minimal amount of all available fully supervised data DL to refine the general SAM into an expert pseudo label generator Scalpel-SAM. To achieve this, we inject a Hierarchical MoE Adapter Aθ into the last two Transformer modules following the ViT encoder EΦ of SAM. Stage One: Knowledge Distillation Based on Hierarchical MoE Adapter The complete training procedure of Stage One is detailed in Algorithm 1, and its architecture is illustrated in Figure 2. Algorithm 1 Stage 1: Knowledge Distillation via Hierarchical MoE Adapter Require: Frozen SAM ViT Encoder EΦ, Trainable MoE Adapter Aθ (with Router Rθ and Experts E(i) θ ), Small fully supervised dataset DL = {(I, Mgt)}, Sparsity weight λsparse. Ensure: Trained adapter parameters θ∗. 1: θ ←InitializeAdapterParameters() 2: for each epoch do 3: for each (I, Mgt) ∈DL do 4: x ←PatchEmbed(I) 5: for l = 1 to L do 6: xblock out ←Bl(x) 7: if l > L −2 then 8: xin ←x 9: w ←Rθ(xin) (See Section II-B1) 10: A(l)(xin) ←0 11: for i = 1 to K = 4 do 12: A(l)(xin) ← A(l)(xin) + wi · E(i) θ (xin) (See Section II-B1 & II-B2) 13: x ←xblock out + A(l)(xin) (See Section II-B2) 14: else 15: x ←xblock out 16: Mpred ←Decoder(x) 17: Lmain ←LBCE(Mpred, Mgt)+ LDice(Mpred, Mgt) (See Section II-B3) 18: Lsparse ←LoadBalancingLoss(w) (See Section II-B3) 19: Ltotal ←Lmain + λsparse · Lsparse (See Section II-B3) 20: Update(θ) 21: return θ∗ 1) Dynamic Expert Routing Mechanism: We employ a lightweight routing network R(·) to dynamically compute weights wi for our K parallel experts. We adopt a soft selection mechanism, where the final adapter output is a weighted fusion of all expert outputs Ei(xl). Full formulas are provided in the supplementary material §A-A. 2) White-Box Expert Toolbox: The four neural operators we designed collectively mimic the progressive cognitive chain by which human experts analyze infrared images: (1) Signal Refining, separating suspicious signals from complex back- grounds (PIMDO & SPD); (2) Contextual Confirmation, de- termining signal authenticity based on local context (HPLSM); and (3) Morphological Focusing, delineating the target shape (TGDS) . • Physics-Informed Manifold Diffusion Operator (PIMDO) To mimic the first step of this chain (refining signals), we pro- pose the PIMDO operator, which we formulate as a learnable anisotropic diffusion process. Its continuous form is governed by the PDE: ∂x ∂t = ∇· (c(|∇x|)∇x) (2) The core of PIMDO is an intelligent diffusion controller c(·), which is trained to promote smoothing in regions with gentle gradients (i.e., noise) while suppressing diffusion at the steep gradients of target edges. However, operating solely in the spatial domain is insufficient. In IR-SOT tasks, many high- frequency background clutter exhibit spatial features highly similar to real targets. • Spectral Prism Decoupler (SPD) We propose the SPD op- erator, which aims to decouple the feature map into orthogonal subspaces {zj}, representing different scales and frequency information, using a learnable wavelet-like transform Wana. Then, a spectral attention module Mspec(·) automatically identifies and enhances the subspaces most likely to contain the target signal while suppressing those that contain clutter. Finally, the feature map is reconstructed through the inverse transform Wsyn: x′ l = Wsyn({αjzj}J j=1), where α = Mspec({zj}) (3) However, static decoupling fails in the highly dynamic and non-homogeneous backgrounds of infrared images (e.g., sky vs. ground clutter), which necessitates the adaptive mechanism introduced next. • Hyper-Parameterized Local Statistics Modulator (HPLSM) This operator endows standard convolutions with environmental awareness capabilities. It contains a hypernetwork Hψ(·), which analyzes the local statistics of the input feature xl in real-time and dynamically generates an affine transformation parameter pair (γij, βij) for each spatial location (i, j). These parameters then modulate the output of a shared base convolution kernel Convθ: Output(xl)ij = γij ⊙Convθ(xl)ij + βij (4) At this point, the target signal has been largely refined, but precise localization in the final step remains a challenge. • Topology-Guided Deformable Sampler (TGDS) We de- sign the TGDS, which employs an offset field prediction network Goff(·), allowing deformable convolutions to actively and non-grid-like capture the target. More importantly, we in- troduce a crucial topological regularization term Ltopo, which encourages the sampled points pk + ∆pk to form a continuous structure that aligns with the target’s geometric shape. The overall offset learning objective is: Loffset = Ltask + λtopo · Ltopo(pk + ∆pk) (5) 3) Training Objectives: The total loss Ltotal consists of a main task loss Lmain and an auxiliary sparsity loss Lsparse. The main loss is a standard weighted sum of BCE and Dice: Lmain = λbce · LBCE(Mpred, Mgt) + λdice · LDice(Mpred, Mgt) (6) The sparsity loss Lsparse is a standard load balancing loss to encourage expert specialization: Lsparse = α · K K X i=1 fi · Pi (7) where fi and Pi are the selection frequency and average probability for expert i, respectively. Stage Two: Knowledge Transfer for Lightweight Deploy- ment While the expert teacher model from Stage One solves the Challenges 1 and 2, its massive size make it completely un- suitable for practical deployment (Challenge 3). Therefore, we designed Stage Two, with the target of transferring the knowl- edge from the upstream teacher model into a lightweight, efficient, and prompt-free downstream model Sψ. 1) Pseudo Label Generation by Expert Teacher: We em- ploy the expert teacher to generate pseudo-masks M pseudo j for the entire dataset Dall = DL ∪DU, treating even labeled samples as unlabeled by disregarding their ground truths. For each image Ij, we perform a forward pass to obtain the pseudo label: M pseudo j = EΦ(Ij; Aθ∗) (9) Thus, we construct a large pseudo label dataset Dpseudo = (Ij, M pseudo j )M j=1, which will serve as the sole source of supervision for the downstream model. 2) Downstream Model Training: After obtaining the pseudo label dataset Dpseudo, we select a lightweight network Sψ suitable for IR-SOT as the downstream student model. We train this downstream model Sψ from scratch, enabling it to learn to fit the pseudo labels generated by the expert teacher. 3) Optimization Objective Update: During the training pro- cess of the second stage, we only use the main task loss Lmain. This loss function is designed to minimize the difference between the predicted mask Mpred of the downstream model Sψ and the pseudo label Mpseudo generated by the expert teacher. As in stage one, Lmain is the weighted sum of BCE and Dice loss: Lmain = λbce · LBCE(Mpred, Mpseudo) + λdice · LDice(Mpred, Mpseudo) (10) where Mpseudo ∈Dpseudo. It is worth noting that the auxiliary sparsity loss Lsparse is no longer used here , as the MoE adapter does not participate in the training of this stage. III. EXPERIMENT A. Implementation Details We conduct experiments on four public datasets: SIRST3 [12], NUAA-SIRST [4], NUDT-SIRST [8], and IRSTD-1K [13]. We employ standard metrics nIoU, mIoU, Pd, Fa and our performance recovery rate : the performance ratio of our 10% data method against the 100% data baseline—to quantify data efficiency. We compare our two-stage semi-supervised paradigm (using 10% data) against two key baselines: (1) the fully supervised paradigm as a theoretical upper bound, and (2) the SOTA point-supervised paradigm, PAL[14]. We apply these paradigms to eight SOTA model (ACM [4], ALCNet [5], MLCL-Net [6], ALCL-Net [7], DNANet [8], GGL-Net [9], UIUNet [10], and MSDA-Net [11]). We use PyTorch with a ViT-h SAM backbone and train on 8×A100- 80G GPUs. All implementation details and hyperparameters are provided in the Supplementary Material. B. Results 1) Validation of Paradigm Necessity: To validate our two- stage design, we benchmark against two pivotal baselines in Table III: (A) Direct Training on 10% Data: Training the student from scratch using only the 10% labeled subset (DL) leads to significant performance drops. This confirms that 10% data is statistically insufficient for learning robust representa- tions, inevitably causing overfitting. Our method circumvents this by using the expert teacher to propagate knowledge to unlabeled data, effectively amplifying the supervision signal. (B) Teacher Inference: Remarkably, our lightweight student matches or even surpasses the heavy Scalpel-SAM teacher. This demonstrates successful knowledge transfer: the student effectively internalizes the teacher’s complex physical priors into a compact representation, resolving the dilemma between model capability and deployment efficiency. 2) Comparison with Fully Supervised Methods: As quan- tified in Table II, our paradigm demonstrates exceptional data efficiency. Surprisingly, using only 10% of labeled data, our method not only approaches but also surpasses the perfor- mance of fully supervised counterparts. Notably, the perfor- mance under fully supervised training is often regarded as an upper bound. To date, no other semi-supervised paradigm has approached, let alone exceeded this fully supervised baseline. In ad- dition, in Figure 3, we present qualitative comparisons of segmentation results produced by different methods. 3) Ablation Study: a) Advancement of MoE routing and white-box expert Design: Table IV validates our core adapter design. The results confirm two key points: (1) Dynamic routing signif- icantly outperforms the static average fusion baseline; and (2) our white-box experts substantially outperform generic black- box PEFT baselines (SAM-Adapter, LoRA). This proves the fundamental advantage of our domain-driven design. b) Expert combination effectiveness analysis: We ablated the combination of our four white-box experts, as shown in Table VIII). The results confirm their complementarity: removing any single expert degrades performance, while the full four-expert model (All) achieves the best results. c) Ablation of adapter insertion layers: We ablated the adapter insertion position and number, as shown in Table IX. The experiments confirm our design choice: inserting the MoE Adapter only after the last two ViT blocks yields the best balance of performance and cost. Notably, inserting adapters after all ViT layers performed the poorest, likely because disrupting SAM’s foundational features at shallow layers. d) Ablation of Sparsity Loss Weight (λsparse): We con- ducted an ablation experiment on the weight coefficient λsparse of the auxiliary sparsity loss. As shown in Table X, the chosen value of λsparse = 0.0100 achieves the optimal performance balance across all datasets. IV. RELATED WORK Our work is closely related to IR-SOT [1] and PEFT [15]. The mainstream methods of IR-SOT have evolved from early local contrast measures (LCM) [16] to deep learning-based segmentation networks (such as DNANet [8] and UIUNet [17]). However, most of these methods follow the training from scratch paradigm, failing to leverage the priors of large foundational models and heavily relying on expensive pixel- level annotations. On the other hand, PEFT techniques have been successfully applied to adapt SAM [18]. However, these methods are generally universal black boxes that do not account for the unique physical properties of infrared images during adaptation. V. CONCLUSION We proposed a two-stage knowledge distillation and transfer paradigm to adapt foundation models to specialized, data- scarce domains. This paradigm first refines SAM into an expert teacher (Scalpel-SAM) using our novel Hierarchical MoE Adapter, which is composed of four white-box physical opera- tors. It then transfers this knowledge to a lightweight, prompt- free downstream model. Experiments show this achieves or surpasses fully supervised SOTA performance with only 10% of labeled data. More importantly, the domain-principle-driven PEFT methodology we propose offers a promising pathway for extending the capabilities of foundational models to other specialized domains, such as medical imaging. {kb}/新论文/2026-10-24/Degraded_Infrared_Sm.text: Degraded Infrared Small Object Detection via Degradation-Adapted Physics-Guided Restoration Xinkai Lu1,3, Wenjun Chen1, Yi Li2⋆, Yi Chang1, and Luxin Yan1 1 National Key Lab of Multispectral Information Intelligent Processing Technology, School of Artificial Intelligence and Automation, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China 2 School of Ocean Engineering, Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University, Shenzhen, China 3 Yichang Testing Technique Research Institute, Yichang, China luxinkai6573@163.com, {wjchen, yichang, yanluxin}@hust.edu.cn, li_yi@tsinghua.edu.cn Abstract. Infrared small object detection has made significant progress in recent years. However, degradations such as fog and nonuniformity can suppress target-background contrast, substantially increasing detection difficulty. Existing methods mainly rely on image restoration as prepro- cessing, but they are typically designed for specific degradation types and fail to generalize to varying degradations. To alleviate this, we pro- pose DAISOD, a degradation-adapted infrared small object detection framework for robust detection under different degradations. DAISOD first identifies the type and severity of degradations, then adapts the processing via dedicated branches, and finally fuses the results for sub- sequent detection. Moreover, a physics-guided restoration mechanism is incorporated to explicitly estimate degradation parameters and remove degradation effects through physical models, avoiding excessive restora- tion that may erase small targets. Moreover, we construct a degraded in- frared small object detection dataset covering diverse degradation types and levels. Extensive experiments show that DAISOD outperforms state- of-the-art methods under various degradation conditions. Keywords: Degraded Infrared Object Detection · Degradation-adapted Restoration · Physical Model Guidance. 1 Introduction Infrared small object detection (ISOD) plays a crucial role in unmanned surveil- lance and perception systems [3, 27] and has attracted extensive research atten- tion. However, degradations such as fog and nonuniformity are ubiquitous in real-world applications, significantly deteriorating infrared image quality and posing severe challenges to small object detection. Fog-induced atmospheric ⋆Corresponding author. arXiv:2608.09311v2 [cs.CV] 16 Aug 2026 2 X. Lu et al. Fig. 1. Comparison of detection pipelines under degraded conditions. (a)-(b) Fixed task-specific pipelines in existing methods limit generalization across diverse degra- dations. (c) Our DAISOD dynamically adapts physics-guided branches through an adaptive weighting mechanism for robust detection. scattering [19, 12] and nonuniform background interference both lead to pro- nounced contrast degradation, which severely suppresses the already limited target-background separability in infrared imagery. As a result, reliable feature extraction becomes more difficult, causing substantial performance degradation in ISOD. To address detection under complex degradations, existing methods can be mainly classified into two categories: image-level methods [21, 14, 18, 24, 6] and feature-level methods [29, 17, 11, 8]. Image-level methods explicitly incorporate image restoration as a preprocessing step to remove degradation effects [24, 6]. Although promising performance has been achieved, these methods are usually designed only for a specific type of degradation and thus struggle to general- ize across different degradation scenarios [30, 2]. More critically, due to their extremely small scale and weak signals, infrared small objects are statistically entangled with degradations, making direct end-to-end restoration prone to erod- ing vulnerable target signals [25, 8]. In contrast, feature-level approaches attempt to alleviate degradation effects by learning degradation-robust representations in the feature space [13, 8, 23]. However, infrared small object detection relies on inherently extremely sub- Degraded Infrared Small Object Detection 3 tle target-background distinctions [9, 23], which can be easily overwhelmed by strong degradations. Furthermore, the highly distinct characteristics of various degradations make it particularly challenging to learn unified and robust feature representations directly from degraded images, thereby limiting generalization across multiple conditions [30, 2]. The above observations highlight a central challenge in ISOD under complex environments: suppressing diverse degradations without damaging inherently weak target signals. To this end, we propose a degradation-adapted infrared small object detection framework, termed DAISOD, which performs degradation-specific restoration guided by corresponding physical models to precisely remove degra- dation interference while preserving target information [24, 6]. Specifically, the proposed framework first analyzes the degradation type and severity in the input infrared images and performs degradation-adapted, physics- guided image restoration to handle diverse degradation scenarios. The restora- tion network estimates key parameters of physical degradation models, enabling explicit and controllable removal of degradation effects while preserving small ob- ject information [24]. To further enhance detection robustness and generalization, a feature-level contrastive loss is incorporated to improve the discriminability of learned representations [2]. The framework is optimized using a staged strategy: the restoration branches are first pretrained, after which the adaptive fusion head and detector are jointly optimized for ISOD under complex environments. In addition, a degraded infrared small object detection dataset with multiple degradation types and severity levels is constructed via physics-based simulation to support comprehensive evaluation. The main contributions are summarized as follows. – We address the challenge of diverse and uncertain degradations in infrared small object detection by proposing a unified degradation-adapted frame- work, termed DAISOD, which jointly handles fog and nonuniformity within a single model. – We introduce a physics-guided degradation-adaptive restoration module that explicitly estimates physical degradation parameters and removes degra- dation effects through physical modeling, enabling effective suppression of degradations while preserving small object information. – We construct a degraded infrared small object detection dataset via physics- based simulation with multiple degradation types and severity levels, on which extensive experiments demonstrate the superior robustness of DAISOD under diverse degradation conditions. 2 Methodology 2.1 Overall Architecture In this work, we focus on the challenging problem of infrared small object de- tection under heterogeneous degradations. The crux lies in the statistical am- biguity between uncertain degradation patterns and vulnerable small targets, 4 X. Lu et al. Fig. 2. Architecture of the proposed DAISOD. The framework integrates a physics- guided degradation-aware network (left) and a detection network (right). The for- mer utilizes parallel estimators to infer physical parameters. Crucially, it employs a degradation-aware estimator to explicitly perceive the degradation context, dynami- cally modulating the contribution of each physics-guided branch for precise adaptation. The latter employs contrastive learning to align restored features with the clean do- main while distancing them from the degraded domain, ensuring degradation-invariant representations. which causes conventional blind restoration methods to inadvertently erode tar- get signals. To tackle this, we introduce DAISOD (Fig. 2), a framework designed to break this ambiguity via physics-guided constraints and feature alignment. Specifically, the physics-guided degradation-aware network explicitly estimates degradation parameters to prevent the network from misinterpreting targets as interference, while the contrastive domain alignment detection network enforces feature-level consistency with the clean domain, ensuring that the restored tar- gets are statistically robust for detection. 2.2 Physics-Guided Degradation-Aware Network Real-world infrared images suffer from coupled degradations. Blind end-to-end restoration risks eroding small targets by treating these as generic noise. To address this, we decouple restoration via physics-guided branches, transforming black-box mappings into transparent parameter estimation. Parametric Nonuniformity Correction. Existing scene-based correction methods often rely on strong motion assumptions, failing in static scenarios, while pure end-to-end deep networks are prone to overfitting. To address this, we propose a hybrid correction scheme that embeds parametric priors into a lightweight deep network. We model the degradation as an additive nonunifor- mity field B(x), formulated as I(x) = J(x) + B(x). Instead of predicting a pixel-wise map, we constrain B(x) using a globally smooth bivariate polynomial Degraded Infrared Small Object Detection 5 surface. For a pixel at coordinate x = (x, y), the bias is defined as: B(x) = D X i=0 D−i X j=0 αi,jxiyj = p(x)⊤α (1) We employ a lightweight coefficient estimator (ResNet-18) to regress the global coefficient vector α. The corrected image is strictly obtained by Jnuc = I −B(x), which effectively removes low-frequency bias while preserving high-frequency target structural details. Physics-Based Defogging. Similarly, for atmospheric scattering, tradi- tional priors are inapplicable to single-channel infrared images, while blind restora- tion networks often lack physical constraints. To ensure restoration fidelity, we adhere to the physical formation model governed by Koschmieder’s law: I(x) = J(x)t(x) + A(1 −t(x)). We employ a U-Net-based fog estimator to estimate the transmission map t(x) and atmospheric light A. The fog-free com- ponent Jfog is then physically recovered via the process of explicit inversion. Jfog(x) = I(x) −A t(x) + A (2) This explicit decoupling ensures that the restoration adheres to physical laws, avoiding intensity distortion. Degradation-Aware Adaptive Fusion. Direct concatenation of multi- branch outputs inevitably introduces information redundancy and conflicting artifacts, as the network struggles to differentiate valid restoration from residual degradations across channels. To mitigate this, we propose a weighted concat fusion strategy. Specifically, the original input I, nonuniformity-corrected Jnuc, and defogged Jfog are first modulated by the degradation-aware weights ω to suppress invalid branches explicitly. The weighted features are then concate- nated and fused via a 3-layer convolutional network. This mechanism acts as a soft feature selection process, ensuring that only complementary, high-quality information is integrated into the final output J. 2.3 Contrastive Domain Alignment and Optimization To bridge the domain gap between restored and clean features, we introduce a contrastive domain alignment regularization mechanism, which is jointly opti- mized with the reconstruction and detection objectives. Motivation and Contrastive Domain Alignment Construction. Un- like generic contrastive representation learning, our objective is not to calibrate an absolute feature distance or discriminate image identities. Feature distances are representation-dependent and may vary considerably across network layers and degradation conditions. Instead, we focus on the relative domain relation- ship: the restored representation should be closer to its clean counterpart than to the corresponding degraded observation. 6 X. Lu et al. For each training sample, we construct a content-aligned triplet in which the restored image J is treated as the anchor, the clean ground-truth image Jgt as the positive, and the corresponding degraded input I as the paired neg- ative. Since these three images share the same scene content and small target, their relative feature distances primarily characterize degradation-induced dis- crepancies rather than unrelated semantic differences. Motivated by ratio-based contrastive regularization in image restoration [26, 31], we define the contrastive domain alignment loss as Lcda = X l ωl ∥ϕl(J) −ϕl(Jgt)∥1 ∥ϕl(J) −ϕl(I)∥1 + ϵ, (3) where ϕl denotes the feature representation extracted from the l-th selected layer, ωl is the corresponding layer weight, and ϵ is a small constant for numerical stability. The numerator measures the positive distance between the restored and clean representations, while the denominator measures the negative distance between the restored and degraded representations. Minimizing Lcda reduces the clean-domain distance relative to the degraded-domain distance, thereby encouraging the restored representation to be closer to the clean reference than to the degraded input. Comparison with Existing Contrastive Objectives. Different from ex- isting contrastive objectives such as InfoNCE [20], the adopted distance-ratio formulation relies on a content-consistent paired negative rather than instance discrimination over a large negative set. Applying InfoNCE to our setting would typically require additional in-batch or memory-bank negatives. Using infrared images from different scenes as such negatives may introduce variations in scene content, background structure, and target location, causing the learned rela- tion to be dominated by semantic differences rather than degradation-induced discrepancies. Moreover, InfoNCE introduces additional dependence on the con- struction of the negative set and the selection of the temperature hyperparame- ter. Moreover, compared with the standard triplet loss [22], which imposes a fixed additive margin, the distance ratio provides a scale-adaptive relative constraint by normalizing the positive distance with the corresponding paired negative dis- tance. This avoids applying a common absolute margin to heterogeneous feature layers and degradation conditions. In addition, the ratio-based objective gen- erally remains active as long as the positive distance is nonzero, whereas the standard margin-based triplet loss becomes inactive once its prescribed margin is satisfied. Therefore, this formulation is selected because it is consistent with our paired restoration setting, rather than as a universally superior replacement for other contrastive objectives. 2.4 Overall Loss and Implementation Details Overall Loss Function. The contrastive term is used as a relative feature-space regularizer rather than an independent restoration objective. Specifically, the

{kb}/Mamba多模态/Adv-Camou_An_Emissivity-ba.text: 1 > REPLACE THIS LINE WITH YOUR MANUSCRIPT ID NUMBER (DOUBLE-CLICK HERE TO EDIT) < Adv-Camou: An Emissivity-based Physical Dynamic Adversarial Patch for Infrared Attack Zhuo Chen, Xu Zheng, Runyun He, Tuoyu Liu, Kaixuan Ding, Yufei Ge, Yijing Song, Tingting Shi, Haining Ji, Pinghua Tang, Haifeng Cheng, Xikun Hu, Dongqing Liu Abstract—With the widespread application of infrared object detection technologies in military domains, intelligent infrared adversarial camouflage capabilities have become critical. Existing physical attack methods predominantly employ static thermal suppression strategies, suffering from limited environmental adaptability, insufficient attack robustness, and inadequate visual concealment. This study proposes Adv-Camou, an emissivity-based physical dynamic adversarial patch that achieves paradigm-shifting advancements from static to dynamic attacks through algorithm-material co-innovation. First, a multi- level loss function based on feature confusion mechanisms is designed to deceive detectors by attenuating target saliency and enforcing background feature alignment. Second, adaptive physical transformations and differentiable binarization optimization are integrated to address physical robustness and realizability constraints. A 6×4 array of reversible electrochromic emissivity device is developed and tested across a range of background scenarios, enabling scene-adaptive dynamic camouflage through independent unit control. Experiments demonstrate that this method achieves 95.59% attack success rate (ASR), reducing average precision (AP) by 60.51%. Physical validations show that static adversarial patches attain 76.55% average ASR under multi-view, multi-range, and multi-spectral conditions, while dynamic patches enhance ASR up to 91.55% in complex environments (wilderness/urban) through adaptive switching. The seamless digital-to-physical transfer via tunable emissivity devices transcends the limitations of traditional static camouflage by establishing a dynamic infrared regulation capability. This advancement enhances the battlefield survivability of military assets and demonstrates transformative potential for adaptive camouflage in practical combat scenarios. Index Terms—Adversarial patch, dynamic emissivity modulation, reversible electrochromic emissivity device, adaptive camouflage This work was supported in part by the Innovation Research Foundation of National University of Defense Technology (Innovation Research Foundation of NUDT), and in part by Hunan Provicial Innovation Foundation for Postgraduate. (Corresponding author: Dongqing Liu). Zhuo Chen and Xu Zheng are co-first authors. Haining Ji and Pinghua Tang are with School of Physics and Optoelectronics, Xiangtan University, Xiangtan, Hunan 411105, China. Xikun Hu is with College of Electronic Science, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, Hunan 410073, China. This article has supplementary downloadable material available at xx, provided by the authors. I. INTRODUCTION hermal infrared object detection has emerged as a cornerstone technology in modern intelligent perception systems, spanning critical domains such as autonomous navigation, all-weather surveillance, search and rescue, and defense reconnaissance. Unlike visible-light sensors that rely on reflected ambient illumination, thermal infrared sensors capture long-wave infrared (LWIR, 8–14 μm) radiation emitted directly by objects as governed by the Stefan-Boltzmann law. Empowered by rapid advancements in deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) [1][2][3], modern infrared detectors achieve remarkable precision under degraded visual conditions, including total darkness, dense fog, and heavy smoke. However, deep neural networks are inherently vulnerable to adversarial examples—inputs perturbed by imperceptible or physically structured patterns that induce high-confidence misclassifications [4][5]. Investigating physical adversarial attacks against thermal detectors is therefore imperative, both for rigorously evaluating the security boundaries of safety-critical perception pipelines and for developing next-generation intelligent stealth technologies. Over the past decade, physical adversarial attacks in the visible spectrum have been extensively investigated, evolving from localized planar patches [6][7][8] to wearable 3D- modeled garments [9][10]. Nevertheless, directly transferring visible-light adversarial paradigms to the thermal infrared domain remains fundamentally constrained by discrepancies in imaging physics. While visible-light cameras resolve high- frequency spatial textures across three chromatic channels (RGB), thermal imagers record single-channel grayscale intensity maps that reflect surface temperature and material emissivity distributions. Consequently, existing infrared physical attack methodologies predominantly rely on static thermal suppression or localized temperature manipulation [11][12][13], which encounter three fundamental bottlenecks in open-world deployment: Lack of Environmental Adaptability: Static adversarial patches [14][15][16] feature fixed spatial topologies optimized for specific training distributions. When targets traverse heterogeneous environments—such as transitioning from structured urban streetscapes with strong mid-frequency architectural contours to cluttered wilderness terrains dominated by high-frequency foliage—the static perturbation fails to adapt to shifting background feature activations, T 2 > REPLACE THIS LINE WITH YOUR MANUSCRIPT ID NUMBER (DOUBLE-CLICK HERE TO EDIT) < leading to severe degradation in attack efficacy. Physical Instability and Digital-to-Physical Degradation: Approaches utilizing active heating elements (e.g., miniature bulbs [12] or resistive heating films) or phase-change temperature- controlled materials [13][17] suffer from inevitable thermal diffusion, ambient convective heat loss, and rapid power depletion. These factors blur the sharp boundaries required for high-frequency adversarial patterns and introduce uncontrollable thermal drift. Conversely, passive emissivity- based materials offer superior edge definition but can only represent discrete binary or tertiary states, creating a substantial optimization gap between continuous digital gradients and discrete physical fabrication. Limited Cross- Architecture Transferability: Many existing infrared attacks employ black-box heuristic optimizers (e.g., Particle Swarm Optimization or Differential Evolution) tailored to specific geometric primitives [18][19][20] or single-model gradient descent [21]. These methods primarily perturb shallow local responses without disrupting deep semantic representations, resulting in poor transferability across diverse detection paradigms (e.g., from anchor-based single-stage detectors to region-proposal two-stage networks and global-attention Transformers). Recent breakthroughs in nanophotonics and functional materials have enabled dynamic thermal camouflage through reversible electrochromic emissivity modulation [22][23][24]. By electrically tuning carrier densities or ion intercalation states, these devices can rapidly modulate surface thermal radiation in real time without altering actual physical temperatures. Inspired by this hardware capability, a compelling scientific question arises: Can we bridge differentiable adversarial optimization in computer vision with reconfigurable emissivity hardware in materials science to achieve scene-adaptive, dynamic physical attacks in the infrared domain? To answer this question, we propose Adv-Camou, an emissivity-based physical dynamic adversarial patch framework that establishes a paradigm shift from static thermal hiding to dynamic, environment-aware adversarial camouflage via algorithm-material co-design. In the digital domain, we formulate a multi-level feature confusion mechanism inspired by contrastive representation learning. Rather than merely minimizing output confidence scores, our loss function simultaneously suppresses intrinsic foreground saliency and aligns perturbed target features with surrounding background distributions in the latent space. To guarantee lossless digital-to-physical realizability on discrete hardware units, we introduce a differentiable binarization optimization strategy leveraging Gumbel-Softmax reparameterization [25] coupled with a Straight-Through Estimator (STE). Furthermore, we integrate complexity-aware Expectation Over Transformation (EOT) [26] and keypoint- driven perspective warping to ensure robustness against multi- view geometric distortions and long-range atmospheric attenuation. In the physical domain, we fabricate a 6 × 4 individually addressable array of reversible electrochromic emissivity devices, enabling real-time pattern switching across diverse operational scenarios. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: Contrastive Feature Confusion Mechanism: We formulate a multi-level feature confusion loss that jointly enforces foreground feature suppression and background latent alignment, substantially enhancing attack efficacy and cross- architecture transferability across CNN- and Transformer- based infrared detectors. Differentiable Discrete Pattern Optimization: We develop a coarse-to-fine differentiable binarization pipeline using Gumbel-Softmax relaxation and complexity-adaptive physical transformations, effectively bridging continuous gradient optimization with discrete, manufacturable emissivity unit arrays. Algorithm-Hardware Co-Design for Dynamic Camouflage: We analyze the frequency- and scale-dependent vulnerability of infrared detectors across heterogeneous scenes and implement a 6×4 reconfigurable electrochromic emissivity array, demonstrating real-world dynamic adversarial pattern switching for the first time. Comprehensive Digital and Physical Evaluations: Extensive experiments demonstrate that Adv-Camou achieves a 95.59% attack success rate (ASR) and reduces average precision (AP) by 60.51% digitally, while physical deployments achieve up to 91.55% ASR across complex wilderness and urban environments via adaptive pattern switching. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work in physical adversarial attacks and cross-modal infrared countermeasures. Section III details the proposed Adv-Camou methodology, including loss formulation, discrete mask optimization, and adaptive physical transformations. Section IV presents comprehensive digital evaluations, cross-model transferability analyses, and real-world static and dynamic physical experiments. Finally, Section V concludes the paper and outlines future research directions. II. RELATED WORKS A. Physical Adversarial Attacks in the Visible Spectrum Physical adversarial attacks aim to generate realizable perturbations that survive real-world imaging pipelines— encompassing illumination fluctuations, viewpoint changes, and sensor noise—to deceive visual perception models. Following early demonstrations on image classifiers using printed eyeglass frames [6], localized stickers [8], and universal patches [7], research shifted extensively toward object detection, which presents greater challenges due to multi-scale regression and dense spatial anchoring. Planar patch-based methods served as the primary testbed: Yang et al. [27] leveraged the EOT framework to synthesize robust patches against YOLO detectors, while Thys et al. [28] optimized printable cardboard patches via backpropagation to evade pedestrian surveillance. To mitigate the visual conspicuousness of high-contrast perturbations, subsequent studies prioritized naturalistic stealthiness and semantic integration. For instance, Zhang and Ma [29] and Guesmi et al. [30] embedded adversarial perturbations into semantic 3 > REPLACE THIS LINE WITH YOUR MANUSCRIPT ID NUMBER (DOUBLE-CLICK HERE TO EDIT) < contexts and artistic textures, respectively, whereas Zhou et al. [31] balanced perceptual realism with deception strength. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and manifold projections have also been widely adopted to synthesize naturalistic patches [32], [33], alongside Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to construct eigenpatches with superior cross- model transferability [34]. Because planar patches fail under severe viewing angles and non-rigid human motion, wearable adversarial camouflage has emerged as a prominent research trajectory. Xu et al. [9] introduced Thin Plate Spline (TPS) transformations to model the non-rigid wrinkling of adversarial T-shirts, while Huang et al. [35] jointly optimized classification and regression branches for universal camouflage. To achieve omnidirectional evasion, Wu et al. [36] and Li et al. [37] developed multi-view optimization frameworks for wearable garments. Pushing the boundaries of spatial coverage, Hu et al. proposed toroidal-cropped repeatable textures (AdvTexture) [10] and 3D-modeled voronoi clothing textures (AdvCaT) [38] to ensure full-angle physical realizability. More recently, Cheng et al. [39] introduced a block-decoupling strategy (DePatch) to alleviate feature coupling interference during physical deployment. Despite these advances, visible-light methods rely exclusively on manipulating high-resolution RGB reflectance, rendering them ineffective against thermal infrared sensors that operate in complete darkness and perceive radiative emission rather than surface color. B. Thermal Infrared and Cross-Modal Physical Attacks To counter thermal infrared detectors, physical perturbations must manipulate either surface temperature or material emissivity inside the LWIR spectrum. Early pioneering efforts by Zhu et al. constructed active thermal perturbations using arrays of miniature incandescent bulbs [12] and QR-code-like thermal insulation clothing [17] to deceive pedestrian detectors. However, active power sources and complex wiring limit wearability and long-term stability. Consequently, passive patches utilizing low-emissivity metals or thermal insulation tapes gained traction. Because the shapes and placements of physical materials are often non-differentiable, zero-order heuristic algorithms have been widely utilized. Wei et al. [11] employed Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to determine the placement of warm and cold stickers, while Hu et al. applied Differential Evolution (DE) and PSO to optimize thermal blocks (AdvIB) [13] and Bézier-curved strips (AdvIC) [18]. Similarly, Tiliwalidi et al. explored geometric primitives (AdvIG) [19] and multi-view grid structures (AdvGrid) [15] via heuristic search. While avoiding gradient computation, these heuristic approaches restrict the perturbation space to simplistic geometric shapes, lacking the structural complexity needed to disrupt deep feature pyramids in cluttered backgrounds. To incorporate gradient information and address multi-sensor fusion systems, white-box shape optimization and visible-infrared cross-modal attacks have recently been explored. Wei et al. proposed learnable infrared patch shapes (AIP) [21] and unified cross-modal boundary patches (UCA) [14] to simultaneously fool RGB and thermal detectors. Building upon this, Hu et al. introduced two-stage cross-modal optimization [20] and bio-inspired leaf-structured patches [16], while Zhu et al. [40] designed 3D-aware infrared car stickers. Nevertheless, existing infrared and cross-modal patches remain fundamentally static after physical fabrication. Fine-grained stripe or grid structures [15], [17] suffer from severe spatial aliasing at extended distances due to the low spatial resolution of thermal focal plane arrays, and static topologies cannot adapt to dramatic shifts in background thermal distributions. In contrast to all prior static schemes, our proposed Adv-Camou integrates differentiable binarized optimization with an electrically tunable electrochromic emissivity array, enabling scene-adaptive dynamic switching and robust multi-scale feature confusion in complex physical environments. Adversarial Camouflage Patch Generation Based on the FLIR ADAS v1.3 dataset, an 8×6 binary patch (0: low-emissivity regions, 1: normal-temperature regions) was applied to the upper body of pedestrians. The feature confusion loss was minimized using a momentum SGD optimizer (batch size: 8, initial learning rate: 0.05). As shown in Fig. 2(a), the generated adversarial patch achieved an ASR of 81.18% against YOLOv5 on the test set, with the AP dropping sharply from 98.28% to 37.77% (a reduction of 60.51%), effectively inducing missed detections (For more details, see Supplementary Material Note 1). The adversarial patch optimized by posture adaptation showed stronger attack effectiveness on the self-made dataset, with an overall ASR of 95.59%. Specifically, the attack performance can still be maintained in extreme side view angles and distant scenes, demonstrating the strong robustness of this method to changes in perspective and scaling. To optimize attack performance, this study systematically evaluated the impact of patch size, grayscale values, and resolution. A black square patch was used as a baseline to validate the effectiveness of the proposed Adv-Camou patches. Experimental results demonstrated that increasing the relative patch size from 0.18 to 0.28 linearly improved the ASR by 42.66% (from 46.77% to 89.43%), as shown in Fig. 2(b). This enhancement stems from larger patches covering broader thermal signature regions, intensifying feature confusion. Notably, under identical size constraints, Adv-Camou achieved 41% higher ASR than the baseline black patch, underscoring the necessity of structural optimization. Grayscale values significantly influenced thermal contrast: extreme values (0 or 1) maximized ASR (82.44% for grayscale 0 and 60.39% for grayscale 1, Fig. 2(c)), while intermediate values (e.g., 0.6) reduced ASR to 34.78% due to similarity with background grayscale (≈0.7). This highlights high contrast as a critical factor for effective attacks. Resolution analysis revealed that an 8×6 grid balanced texture complexity and optimization stability, achieving 74.91% ASR (Fig. 2(d)). Lower resolutions (6×4) degraded ASR by 7.17% due to oversimplified patterns, while higher resolutions (11×9) suffered from local optima issues, reducing ASR by 18%. These findings indicate that patch size and contrast dominate attack strength, while resolution governs pattern optimizability. Through parameter co-optimization (recommended: size ≥0.22, grayscale 0, 8 ×6 resolution), robust attacks with ASR >80% can be achieved in complex infrared scenarios. B. Static Adversarial Camouflage Patch Attack To validate the robustness of Adv-Camou, we compared it with baseline methods—Random Patch, QR Code, AIP, and UCA—under identical perturbation regions. As summarized in Table 1, Adv-Camou achieved an ASR of 81.18% on the test set, significantly outperforming AIP (23.66%) and UCA (21.32%). The AP of YOLOv5 plummeted from 98.28% to 37.77% (a 60.51% reduction), while comparative methods retained AP values above 89% (For more details, see Supplementary Material Note 3). The superior performance of Adv-Camou arises from its multi-scale feature alignment mechanism, which generates structurally complex patterns to disrupt the multi-scale feature fusion process of detection models. In contrast to QR Code-based attacks, Adv-Camou’s sparse binarized structure ensures precise coverage of critical feature attention regions (e.g., shoulders and torso), effectively dismantling the model’s holistic perception of human anatomy (For more details, see Supplementary Material Note 3). QR codes, however, suffer from high-frequency texture distortion at long ranges, while AIP/UCA only locally suppress features without blocking feature propagation pathways. Further tests on a custom dataset (multi-view, multi-distance) demonstrated Adv-Camou’s exceptional adaptability: it achieved 95.59% ASR (Fig. 3), maintaining robust performance under extreme side views (±45°) and long distances (>10 m). In overhead angle experiments (45°/60°), geometric adaptation enabled the patch to counteract target deformations, sustaining precise coverage of key thermal regions under dynamic conditions. These results confirm that Adv-Camou’s structural optimization and feature confusion mechanisms significantly enhance attack robustness in complex surveillance scenarios.

{kb}/Jiang_PhyFusion_Physics-Aware_Infra.text: PhyFusion: Physics-Aware Infrared and Visible Image Fusion via Modality-Specific Physical Priors Haiyang Jiang1, Huiqin Zhang1, Yanduo Zhang1, Jiayi Ma2, Junjun Jiang3, Huabing Zhou1* 1Hubei Key Laboratory of Intelligent Robot, Wuhan Institute of Technology 2Wuhan University 3Harbin Institute of Technology {j864308526,666zhanghuiqin}@gmail.com, ydzhang@wit.edu.cn jyma2010@gmail.com, jiangjunjun@hit.edu.cn, Zhouhuabing@gmail.com Abstract Infrared–visible image fusion (IVIF) aims to combine ther- mal and structural cues into a single image that remains reliable under challenging illumination. The task becomes challenging in real scenes where the two modalities fol- low fundamentally different imaging principles. Most exist- ing methods treat fusion as an appearance-matching prob- lem and overlook these physical differences, leading to fused images that weaken infrared radiative contrast and blur reflectance-driven structures. We present PhyFusion, a physics-aware IVIF framework that brings the imaging principles of both modalities directly into the fusion pro- cess. Two Physical Priors Extractors, guided by the Ra- diative transfer model and the Retinex reflectance model, estimate five physically interpretable components for recon- struction. Among them, emissivity and reflectance provide the most stable and complementary cross-modal cues, and we use these two quantities as explicit guidance signals. A Physics-Guided Fusion Module encodes the physical priors via a DINO backbone, injects multi-level physical features with cross-modal interaction, and modulates fused repre- sentations with global physical context through spatially adaptive normalization. A Physical Consistency Loss fur- ther enforces radiometric and structural coherence during reconstruction. Across multiple public benchmarks, PhyFu- sion consistently produces fused images that retain stronger thermal contrast, preserve finer structural detail, and re- main physically consistent with the underlying sensor imag- ing models, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in both visual quality and downstream vision tasks. *Corresponding author. Introduction Infrared–visible image fusion (IVIF)[1, 15, 38, 47] is a fun- damental technique in computer vision that combines com- plementary information from infrared and visible sensors into a single image with enhanced detail and perception. Visible sensors provide abundant textural and color cues but degrade severely in dark or adverse weather conditions, whereas infrared sensors capture thermal radiation reliably yet lack fine structural information[40–42]. By effectively exploiting complementary information, IVIF delivers richer and more holistic scene representations[44]. Consequently, it has been widely applied in security surveillance[45], mil- itary target detection[20], scene understanding[43], and ad- vanced driver-assistance systems[2]. Despite progress in image fusion [16, 26, 31, 35], most existing methods remain largely physics-agnostic, relying on appearance-based feature extraction while ignoring the physical mechanisms behind image formation. As a result, fused images often exhibit weakened thermal responses and blurred structural details. DRF [9] incorporates Retinex- based priors in the visible domain, yet it does not account for the radiative properties unique to infrared sensing, lim- iting its ability to preserve modality-specific cues. As shown in Fig. 1, the contrast between different fusion results reveals the central role of modality-specific physi- This CVPR Findings paper is the Open Access version, provided by the Computer Vision Foundation. Except for this watermark, it is identical to the accepted version; the final published version of the proceedings is available on IEEE Xplore. 4993 cal priors. Infrared appearance is primarily determined by emissivity, which results in dark low-emissivity sky and strong radiative responses on metal pole, pedestrians, and road boundaries, with temperature modulating the magni- tude of this radiation. Visible appearance, in contrast, is governed by reflectance, which provides stable material- dependent structure on the road, buildings, and vegetation, while illumination affects only global brightness. As shown in Fig. 1(b), physics-agnostic fusion methods fail to pre- serve these modality-specific signatures, producing over- brightened sky, weakened cloud contrast, and smoothed re- flective surfaces. These observations motivate the need for a fusion framework that explicitly models emissivity in in- frared imaging and reflectance in visible imaging, rather than relying solely on appearance-driven statistics. Recent developments in intrinsic image decomposi- tion [7, 34] and thermodynamic modeling [2, 8, 19] further support this idea. Retinex-based methods [30, 32, 36, 46] decompose visible images into reflectance and illumination layers, while thermodynamic studies model the emissiv- ity–temperature relationship that underlies infrared imag- ing. Together, these findings suggest that modality-specific physical priors can serve as reliable guides for adaptive and interpretable image fusion. Building on these insights, we propose PhyFusion, a physics-aware infrared–visible fusion framework grounded in the imaging principles of both modalities. Two Phys- ical Prior Extractors, informed by the Radiative transfer model and the Retinex reflectance model, estimate five physical components for reconstruction: emissivity, tem- perature, and thermal radiation for the infrared modality, and reflectance and illumination for the visible modality. Among these components, emissivity and reflectance pro- vide the most stable and complementary cues for fusion, and we use them as the primary guidance signals. The Physics-Guided Fusion Module encodes these two priors using a DINO backbone to obtain multi-level physical fea- tures and a global physical representation. Cross-modal interaction integrates the multi-level physical features into the source-image streams, and spatially adaptive normaliza- tion injects the global physical representation into the fused features. A Restormer decoder, together with a Physical Consistency Loss, reconstructs the final output while main- taining radiometric and structural coherence across diverse scenes. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: • We propose PhyFusion, a physics-aware infrared–visible image fusion framework that, to the best of our knowl- edge, is the first to explicitly integrate the imaging physics of both sensors as modality-specific priors into the fusion process. • We develop two Physical Priors Extractors to estimate the emissivity–temperature–thermal (E, T, V) and re- flectance–illumination (R, L) components, and design a Physics-Guided Fusion Module that injects the two key priors, emissivity and reflectance, through cross-modal interaction and spatially adaptive normalization. • Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that PhyFusion significantly surpasses state-of-the-art fusion algorithms, delivering superior performance in terms of visual quality and effectiveness in high-level vision tasks. 2. Related Work In recent years, deep learning-based image fusion methods have attracted considerable attention owing to the powerful capabilities of neural networks[44]. Early methods primar- ily rely on convolutional architectures. DenseFuse[12] in- troduces convolutional encoders with dual fusion strategies, while NestFuse[13] enhances detail preservation through multi-scale nested connections. More recently, transformer- based approaches have gained increasing attention in im- age fusion. ITFuse[28] introduces alternating feature- interaction and reconstruction modules equipped with resid- ual and cross-modal attention, enabling iterative capture and fusion of salient information. For mis-registration sce- narios, C2RF[27] unifies registration and fusion through commonality mining and contrastive learning; by treating misaligned outputs as hard negatives, it jointly refines de- formation fields and aggregated features, effectively miti- gating ghosting artifacts. In parallel, interpretable fusion networks such as CAMF[25] exploit class-activation map- ping to learn channel-wise importance weights, selectively retaining salient targets and textures while providing post- hoc interpretability. Recently, diffusion-based methods have demonstrated promising performance. HCLFuse[10], for instance, employs a conditional diffusion model with human cognitive laws to improve interpretability. Fur- thermore, some advanced works[37, 42] attempt to lever- age large visual language models to mine semantic infor- mation from images in order to achieve adaptive fusion. While cross-modal feature integration has advanced, cur- rent approaches still overlook the mechanisms behind im- age formation, limiting their fusion performance in complex scenes. Therefore, it is necessary to introduce an innovative adaptive fusion model guided by physical priors. 3. The proposed Method The overall framework of our PhyFusion is illustrated in Fig. 2. The proposed pipeline consists of two princi- pal stages: (I) Physical Priors Extraction (PPE) and (II) Physical Priors Guidance and Fusion (PPGF). First, during the PPE stage, PhyFusion feeds the visible and infrared im- ages into two modality-specific physical priors extractors to extract features with special properties. {kb}/1.pdf.text: Efficient RGB-T Object Detection via Sparse Cross-Modality Fusion Chao Tian1 , Zikun Zhou1⋆, Chao Yang1 , Guoqing Zhu1 , and Zhenyu He1⋆ Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China tianchao@stu.hit.edu.cn, zhouzikunhit@gmail.com, {20b951014,20B951002}@stu.hit.edu.cn, zhenyuhe@hit.edu.cn Abstract. RGB-T detectors leverage the complementary strengths of visible and thermal infrared modalities, achieving robust performance under challenging conditions. Many of them resort to heavy dual back- bones and exhaustive cross-modality fusion across the entire image, lead- ing to impractically high computational costs. We observe that most im- age regions are smooth backgrounds (e.g., sky, ground) that can be easily handled by lightweight single-modality models. In light of this observa- tion, we propose a sparse fusion mechanism for efficient RGB-T detec- tion: first rapidly scanning the image to identify the proposals and then carefully examining the remaining sparse proposals via feature fusion. We propose a two-stage framework to instantiate this mechanism, which performs detection in two stages: 1) a lightweight and modality-specific detection stage that produces high-recall RoIs, and 2) a fusion-driven ex- amination and refinement stage that filters out the false positives and re- fines the bounding boxes. This design enables the detector to adaptively allocate more computational resources to the potential foregrounds, im- proving the efficiency while ensuring detection accuracy. Extensive ex- periments show that our method achieves competitive performance with substantially fewer parameters and lower cost, while maintaining strong scalability to high-resolution images. Keywords: RGB-Thermal infrared · Sparse fusion · Object detection 1 Introduction RGB-Thermal infrared (RGB-T) object detection aims to leverage the comple- mentarity from different modalities to handle various challenging conditions [20, 37], drawing much attention in recent years. Numerous benchmarks [14, 21, 36] and detectors [18,26,37] have been proposed. Detectors based on feature fusion have acquired superior detection performance [25], which typically extract the RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) features using two independent backbones and perform pixel-to-pixel feature fusion [27,33]. However, the computational com- plexity of these powerful RGB-T detectors remains undesirably high, reaching up to hundreds of GFLOPs [5,16,22,25], restricting their practical applicability. ⋆Corresponding authors. arXiv:2606.30215v1 [cs.CV] 29 Jun 2026 2 C. Existing powerful RGB-T detectors primarily employ heavy dual backbones and perform sophisticated feature fusion uniformly across the entire image to detect the target objects accurately. Nevertheless, the backgrounds, such as the sky and ground, which generally occupy the majority of the image, are smooth and can be readily distinguished by lightweight models, even when utilizing only a single modality. Hence, processing the backgrounds with a heavy feature ex- tractor and a complex fusion mechanism is unnecessary and highly inefficient. In light of this, an effective strategy for constructing lightweight yet high-precision RGB-T detectors is to pre-filter these simple background regions using compact single-modality models and employ a powerful cross-modality fusion module to process the remaining regions. This is essentially an efficient sparse fusion mech- anism, adaptively allocating more computational resources to potential fore- grounds, as shown in Figure 1 (a). The prerequisite for the sparse fusion mechanism is that the lightweight model can identify potential foregrounds at a high recall rate without unaccept- able mistaken drops. To figure this out, we conduct an analytical experiment with YOLOv8-Large and YOLOv8-Small [28]. Figure 1 (b) presents the Preci- sion–Recall (PR) curves on FLIR [36]. We observe that the lightweight detector achieves a cut-off recall comparable to that of the heavyweight detector, both remarkably close to 100%, when the IoU threshold is 50%. Such a high recall Efficient RGB-T Object Detection via Sparse Cross-Modality Fusion 3 validates the effectiveness of a lightweight model for searching potential fore- grounds, i.e., proposals. This demonstrates the feasibility of the sparse fusion mechanism. Nevertheless, we observe two limitations from the PR curves. First, the PR curve of the lightweight detector remains consistently lower than that of the heavyweight one at IoU=50%. This suggests a high false-positive rate in the preliminary proposals, which therefore requires further verification for accu- rate recognition. Second, the recall drops sharply at IoU=75%, indicating the limited localization accuracy of the lightweight model. These two issues can be effectively mitigated with the robust features derived from cross-modality fusion. In this paper, we instantiate Sparse Fusion mechanism and propose an Efficient RGB-T object Detector, dubbed SFEDet, as illustrated in Figure 1(d). Specifically, we employ two lightweight detectors, one for each modality, serv- ing as region proposal networks (RPNs) to identify potential foreground regions, i.e., Regions of Interest (RoIs), for further detailed examination. Herein, to avoid missing real objects during proposal extraction, we construct the proposal set by taking the union of RoIs from individual modalities. Subsequently, we borrow RoI Align [10] to extract paired RoI features from the two modalities. Despite the high recall of the collected proposals extracted by our RPNs, as shown in Figure 1 (c), the RPNs still suffer from false positives and inaccurate localiza- tion. To accurately filter out false positives and refine coarse bounding boxes, we introduce a Fusion-driven Examination and Refinement (FER) module to process the RoIs for final detection, which performs multi-step feature fusion fol- lowed by step-wise classification and box refinement. In this way, the lightweight RPNs process the entire image preliminarily, while the sophisticated FER mod- ule operates only on sparse RoI features with fixed spatial sizes. This design enables a favorable balance between efficiency and performance. Moreover, due to the sparse fusion mechanism, SFEDet demonstrates excellent scalability for high-resolution images, as the computational complexity of FER depends solely on the number of RoIs, as demonstrated in Figure 1 (e). The implementation of the FER module is crucial to the efficiency and per- formance of our SFEDet. To this end, we introduce a Rolling Convolution op- erator into the FER module to replace the conventional convolution operator, improving its efficiency. Furthermore, we adopt a denoising training strategy to facilitate the FER module to learn to process proposals with large localization errors, consequently improving its detection performance. We conduct elaborate experiments on FLIR, M3FD, and LLVIP datasets, where the SFEDet achieves a balance between efficiency and precision. The main contributions can be sum- marized as follows: – We introduce a sparse fusion mechanism that adaptively allocates greater computational resources to potential foreground regions; it is then instanti- ated within our SFEDet framework, enabling SFEDet to achieve a favorable balance between efficiency and performance. – We propose a fusion-driven examination and refinement method to process the sparse proposals, which effectively filters out the false positives and re- fines the coarse bounding boxes via step-wise feature enhancement. 4 C. Tian et al. – We conduct extensive experiments on popular RGB-T detection benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method and highlighting its scalability for high-resolution images. 2 Related works 2.1 RGB-T Object Detection In recent years, several benchmarks [13,36] have been established and promote the development of the detection area. Some of them, such as M3FD [21] and LLVIP [14], are well aligned and adopted not only in object detection but also in pixel-level image fusion. The algorithms for RGB-T object detection have advanced substantially, evolving from image fusion-based methods [29, 40] and box fusion-based meth- ods [3] to feature fusion-based approaches. Among these, He et al. [11] proposed weighting different modalities according to the information difference measured within their local neighborhoods. Li et al. [15,18] adjusted the fusion weights of RGB and TIR features based on illumination conditions. Hu et al. [12] incorpo- rated edge priors to constrain the fusion process, while ICAFusion [25] employed a cross-attention mechanism for modality guidance. Other studies [37, 43] used box-aligned masks as spatial guidance to achieve more precise fusion. Chen et al. [2, 34] introduced vision transformers into RGB-T object detectors, while Dong [6] employed Mamba [9] to perform feature fusion. In addition, several studies have addressed specific challenges in RGB-T object detection. Tian et al. [27, 38] focused on the non-alignment issue, whereas Zhou et al. [26, 42] in- vestigated the modality imbalance problem, where the RGB and TIR modalities contribute unequally to the fusion results. However, the computational overhead of feature fusion-based RGB-T detectors has received little attention to date. 2.2 Efficient Object Detectors Efficient lightweight detectors have been extensively studied in general object detection. The YOLO [23] series is well known for enabling real-time detec- tion. Early versions [1, 24] are anchor-based, which makes both training and deployment relatively complex. Subsequent improvements, such as YOLOX [8] and TOOD [7], introduce dynamic sample assignment, a technique that has been widely adopted in later versions of YOLO [28,30]. YOLOv7 [31] and PP- YOLOE [32] further enhance the network architectures to improve inference speed and overall efficiency. YOLOv10 [30] focuses on eliminating the non- maximum suppression (NMS) post-processing step, which has long been con- sidered a bottleneck in detector acceleration. DETR-like detectors [17, 35, 44] generally achieve higher upper-bound performance but at the cost of increased computational complexity. RT-DETR [41] is a real-time DETR-based detector that strikes a favorable balance between speed and accuracy. This issue has received limited attention in prior studies. Deevi [4] attempts to alleviate the training cost by freezing two backbones; however, the overall computational com- plexity of the model remains unchanged. Addressing this limitation constitutes the primary goal of our work. 3 Method In this section, we present the instantiation of the sparse fusion mechanism, i.e., the SFEDet framework, which performs efficient and accurate RGB-T de- tection through two stages: 1) the first stage takes a quick look at the entire image with lightweight model to filter out the redundant backgrounds while retaining potential foreground regions; 2) the second stage performs detailed examination and refinement within the sparse foreground regions, i.e., the RoIs, to produce the final detection results. Next, we describe the overall framework of SFEDet and detail its key components. 3.1 Overall framework of SFEDet Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework of SFEDet performing detection in two stages. In the first stage, we employ two lightweight detectors serving as independent RPNs to filter out the apparent background regions through pre- liminary detection. We then construct the proposal set by taking the union set of 6 C. Tian et al. proposals from individual modalities. To further reduce redundancy in the pre- liminary detections, we subsequently apply NMS in the union set to get sparse, non-overlapping proposals. With these proposals, we extract the corresponding RGB-T RoI feature pairs from the multi-level FPN features via RoI Align, where each proposal box is used to get spatially aligned features from two modalities. The proposals generated in the first stage typically contain numerous false posi- tives and poorly localized boxes. To address these issues, we further introduce a Fusion-driven Examination and Refinement (FER) module in the second stage. It fuses the RGB and TIR features through multi-step feature enhancement, producing a more robust representation for each RoI and facilitating the sup- pression of false positives. For proposals with inaccurate localization, a step-wise refinement strategy is adopted to progressively refine the bounding boxes. The most computationally intensive component of our SFEDet, i.e., the FER module, is activated only within potential foreground regions. This means that the computational cost depends primarily on the number of RoIs. Consequently, SFEDet exhibits strong scalability when processing high-resolution images. We provide detailed designs of the proposed FER module, the box refinement pro- cedure, and the overall training schedule of SFEDet in the following sections. 3.2 Fusion-driven Examination and Refinement Due to numerous false positives or poorly localized proposals in the first-stage results, we thus design an elaborate Examination and Refinement module based on the cross-modality feature fusion to address this, as illustrated in Figure 2. We deploy an efficient differential-enhanced group-wise fusion (DEGF) to balance the fusion cost and quality. The following multi-step enhancements with auxiliary features ensure a robust representation for each RoI. Differential-enhanced group-wise fusion. This module contains a group- wise cross-modality fusion and a subsequent differential enhancement module. Before fusion, the RoI features from both RGB and TIR modalities are simul- taneously extracted from three stages of the feature pyramid network (FPN) via RoI Align, denoted as FM fpn−i, where M ∈{rgb, tir} and i ∈{1, 2, 3}. Multi-stage features from FPN are then reduced into a cross-stage representa- tion FM fpn ∈RC×5×5 for each proposal, where C denotes the number of channels and 5 represents the RoI spatial size. Core of this module is the group-weighting fusion applied to Frgb fpn and Ftir fpn, as illustrated in Figure 2. After the Ngw-group split along the channel dimen- sion, the weights within each group are predicted separately and shared across the entire group in fusion, which reduces the computational cost. The softmax normalization ensures that the sum of weights equals one for each channel pair. The fused features are denoted as F1 fu.
