In the early stages, traditional methods [4], [5], [6], [7] that heavily rely on assumptions and prior knowledge dom- inated the ISTD ﬁeld. Although these methods achieve good performance, they usually have limited generalization abil- ity. Recently, ISTD methods based on deep learning have demonstrated remarkable success. Some methods based on a convolutional neural network (CNN), such as the ACM [8] and ALCNet [9], achieve high detection speeds but often have limited accuracy. With the signiﬁcant advancements of Transformers and diﬀusion models in computer vision tasks, researchers have started to explore their potential in ISTD tasks, leading to the development of models such as the IAANet [10] built on Transformers and DCFR-Net [11] utiliz- ing diﬀusion models. However, although achieving excellent accuracy, these algorithms suﬀer from a heavier computa- tional burden due to the more complex structures or diﬀusion processes. Given the critical demands for lightweight models with low computational costs in practical ISTD applications, there is an urgent need to develop a more accurate and eﬃcient network to improve detection performance in real- world scenarios. Inspired by the lightweight Mamba structures [12], [13], the main motivation of this article is to develop a more eﬃcient Mamba-based algorithm with high accuracy for ISTD tasks, addressing the limitations of CNN- and Transformer- based architectures. On the one hand, traditional CNN-based methods rely on local receptive ﬁelds, making it diﬃcult to eﬀectively capture long-range dependencies, which is crucial for detecting infrared small targets in complex backgrounds. On the other hand, while Transformer-based methods can model long-range dependencies through global self-attention, their quadratic computational complexity with respect to input resolution often results in high computational costs. In con- trast, Mamba leverages an eﬃcient state-space model (SSM) with linear complexity, enabling it to model long-range depen- dencies while achieving signiﬁcantly lower computational complexity. Speciﬁcally, we ﬁrst introduce a Mamba-based UNet with fewer parameters by processing deep features in a parallel manner based on the UltraLight VM-UNet [14]. This attempt reinforces our belief that the Mamba-based network is a com- pelling and promising exploration for eﬃcient ISTD. Then, the enhanced image and the original image are weighted to be processed by the proposed Mamba-based UNet, which eﬀectively improves the ability of the model to distinguish the dim objects from the cluttered backgrounds. While Mamba excels at modeling long-range dependencies through the SSM, it does not inherently emphasize local spatial saliency. This can be a limitation for ISTD, where subtle and localized spatial information is often the critical factor in distinguishing small targets from complex backgrounds. To address this and optimize feature utilization, we further propose a shared adaptive spatial attention module (SASAM) to reﬁne spatial responses. With this module, diﬀerent types of spatial attention maps are adaptively weighted rather than directly concatenated to generate the ﬁnal spatial attention map, enabling it to complement Mamba’s sequence modeling capabilities while reducing the additional computational cost introduced. Finally, this article proposes an eﬃcient adaptive Mamba network (EAMNet) as shown in Fig. 1 for ISTD tasks. The intention of the EAMNet lies not in proposing a fundamentally new Mamba block structure, but in the way an eﬃcient Mamba variant is introduced into a task-speciﬁc framework for ISTD. This design addresses the limitations of CNN- and Transformer-based architectures, while the newly designed AFM and SASAM modules are speciﬁcally tailored to tackle the unique challenges of this task. In summary, the main contributions of this work are as follows. 1) A Mamba-based UNet with fewer parameters is intro- duced, which processes deep features in parallel. This architecture leverages Mamba to eﬀectively model long- range dependencies while achieving linear complexity, presenting promising potential for eﬃcient ISTD with high accuracy. 2) To better adapt the Mamba structure to the unique characteristics of infrared images, an AFM is proposed by employing an additionally designed subnetwork to predict ﬁlter parameters, allowing for adaptive enhance- ment of infrared images. 3) We propose a SASAM that complements Mamba’s sequence modeling capabilities while producing a more compact and eﬃcient feature representation for spatial attention map generation, further enhancing model per- formance and ensuring eﬃcient feature fusion. The rest of this article is organized as follows. In Section II, we brieﬂy review the related work. In Section III, the proposed EAMNet is introduced in detail. In Section IV, the compara- tive experimental results and analyses are given. Finally, we conclude this article in Section V. II. RELATED WORK A. Infrared Small-Target Detection Early traditional works can be mainly divided into three categories, including ﬁltering-based methods [15], [16], local-contrast-based methods [4], [17], [18], [19], and low- rank-based methods [5], [20], [21]. Although these traditional methods have demonstrated promising results, they are often constrained by predeﬁned assumptions and prior knowledge, making them sensitive to hyperparameters. This sensitivity limits their generalization ability to complex real-world sce- narios, especially in cluttered and noisy environments, making the detection task still challenging in practical applications. To overcome these problems, recent deep learning-based methods have attracted increasing attention due to their powerful feature representation capabilities [10], [11], [22], [23]. The ACM [8] proposes the asymmetric contextual module, which achieves good performance in the host networks of the FPN [24] and the U-Net [25]. Besides, it builds an open single-frame dataset named SIRST to advance the research of the ISTD tasks. The ALCNet [9] introduces an attentional local contrast network that captures relatively long-range contextual inter- actions. To address the interclass imbalance between targets and backgrounds, RDIAN [26] utilizes convolutional layers with various receptive ﬁelds for feature extraction, achieving outstanding performance on key metrics. The DNA-Net [27] proposes a dense nested attention network with a dense nested interactive module and a cascaded channel and spatial attention module (SAM), enabling progressive interaction between high- and low-level features while adaptively enhancing multilevel features. The RPCANet [28] enhances the interpretability of the ISTD task by combining network emulations with model- driven ISTD approaches, producing trustworthy results. The IAANet [10] proposes a coarse-to-ﬁne architecture based on a Transformer that initially uses the RPN [29] to identify coarse object regions, which are then reﬁned with a per- pixel prediction in each proposed area. The DCFR-Net [11] ﬁrst super-resolves infrared targets through a diﬀusion-based continuous high-resolution branch, then leverages high-quality feature representation to enhance ISTD. However, these methods often struggle to balance accuracy and eﬃciency, with higher accuracy typically coming at the expense of increased network complexity and computational burden. In contrast, our work focuses on developing an eﬃ- cient framework based on the advanced Mamba structure, which explores a promising direction for ISTD and is impor- tant for real-world applications. Besides, diﬀerent from spiking neural network (SNN)-based models [30], [31], [32], [33], which focus on biologically inspired temporal dynamics, our proposed method is designed for conventional frame-based infrared images and prioritizes lightweight implementation and real-time performance using a Mamba-based UNet architec- ture. B. Mamba in Vision Tasks Recently, SSMs have attracted growing interest among researchers in various computer vision tasks [34], [35], [36], [37]. Compared to the quadratic complexity of the self- attention mechanism in Transformers, SSMs achieve excellent performance with linear complexity, which is essential for the development of lightweight models. Mamba [12] intro- duces a selection mechanism to structured SSMs and has demonstrated promising eﬃciency and eﬀectiveness in various long-sequence modeling tasks [38], [39]. III. PROPOSED METHOD In this section, we introduce the EAMNet, an eﬃcient Mamba-based network for ISTD tasks. As shown in Fig. 1, the overall architecture of the model consists of three key components: 1) a Mamba-based UNet for eﬃcient ISTD (Section III-A); 2) an AFM to enhance the boundaries and visibility of infrared targets (Section III-B); and 3) a SASAM to enhance target information and suppress visually similar background information (Section III-C). Speciﬁcally, the Mamba-based UNet mainly consists of six encoder layers and six decoder layers. The ﬁrst three encoder layers focus on extracting shallow features and providing low- level details through a 3 × 3 convolution layer, with each layer followed by GroupNorm [43], a max-pooling operation, and the GeLU activation function [44]. In the deeper encoder layers, we introduce an eﬃcient Mamba block that adapts the high eﬃciency of the Mamba structure to ISTD tasks. Each Mamba block is followed by GroupNorm, a max-pooling operation, and the GeLU activation function, except for the ﬁnal layer, which is only followed by the GeLU activation function. This design enhances feature representation, achiev- ing both high eﬃciency and superior detection performance in complex infrared images. The decoder layers almost maintain the same setup as the encoder layers, enabling eﬀective feature reconstruction while beneﬁting from the eﬃcient Mamba block. A. Eﬃcient Parallel Mamba Block Recently, Mamba has gained signiﬁcant attention in various vision tasks for its superior computational eﬃciency, reduced GPU memory usage, and strong ability to model long-range dependencies. Unlike CNNs, which struggle to capture global context, or Transformers, which suﬀer from quadratic com- plexity, Mamba achieves linear complexity while maintaining strong modeling capacity. Leveraging these advantages, we incorporate the Mamba architecture as a core component in the design of our eﬃcient ISTD framework. Inspired by the UltraLight VM-UNet [14], we introduce the Mamba in a parallel manner, which improves feature extraction eﬃciency. We introduce the eﬃcient parallel Mamba block in Encoder 4-6 and Decoder 4-6, which helps to model long-range depen- dencies for ISTD. Therefore, eﬀective data augmentation of the original images is essential to improve algorithm performance in detecting these targets. Given the eﬀectiveness of image ﬁlters in processing complex images, we utilize three ﬁlters, including Gamma, Contrast, and Sharpen ﬁlters, for their suitability in enhancing infrared images, to facilitate ISTD tasks. First, these ﬁlters are theoretically suitable for enhancing infrared images [45], [46], as they correspond to key aspects of infrared target visibility: brightness, contrast, and edge clarity. Our design builds upon traditional image enhancement methods but extends them in a more ﬂexible and adaptive way. Speciﬁcally, rather than relying on ﬁxed hyperparameters, we propose a CNN-based prediction subnetwork that dynamically estimates the parameter for each ﬁlter, conditioned on the input image content. Second, each ﬁlter involves only a single parameter to be predicted, which makes the approach computationally eﬃcient and simpliﬁes the CNN-based pre- diction subnetwork with fewer parameters, making it suitable for real-time or resource-constrained applications. Moreover, all three ﬁlters are diﬀerentiable, which allows the entire enhancement module to be seamlessly integrated into the end- to-end learning pipeline. This design enables the subnetwork to be optimized jointly with the rest of the network through standard backpropagation in an adaptive, data-driven manner. Shared Adaptive SAM Eﬀective fusion of multistage and multiscale information is critical for improving the performance of various computer vision tasks [50], [51], [52], [53], [54]. To further enhance model performance and ensure eﬃcient feature fusion, we propose the SASAM, which is designed to enable the model to focus on relevant features during the fusion process while reducing the inﬂuence of less relevant information. As shown in Fig. 4, this module is applied to the outputs of the ﬁrst ﬁve encoder layers with all the learnable parameters shared. Besides, our model only focuses on spatial attention, given the unique characteristics of infrared small-target images, where targets are often small, dim, and occupy only a few pixels. In such cases, channel attention may be less eﬀective in distinguishing small targets from the background, while spatial attention is more beneﬁcial as it directly empha- sizes the location of the target, which is crucial for ISTD tasks. Additionally, this approach introduces fewer parameters and computational complexity, ensuring the model remains eﬃcient. Loss Function The proposed EAMNet follows a supervised learning frame- work, requiring labeled training data with binary maps serving as ground-truth annotations to guide the learning process. During training, the EAMNet is optimized using the BceDice loss function, which combines the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss and the Dice loss to enhance the learning process. The BCE loss is widely used for pixel-wise classiﬁca- tion tasks, eﬀectively handling small-target regions, which is deﬁned as LBCE = −1 N N X i=1  yi log ˆyi + (1 −yi) log (1 −ˆyi)  (11) where yi represents the ground-truth label, ˆyi is the predicted result, and N is the total number of pixels. The Dice loss is eﬀective in handling class imbalance scenarios by quantifying the overlap between predicted and ground-truth masks. It is formulated as follows: LDice = 1 − 2 PN i=1 yiˆyi + ϵ PN i=1 yi + PN i=1 ˆyi + ϵ (12) where ϵ is a small constant to prevent numerical instability. In summary, the ﬁnal optimal object for the proposed model is formulated as follows: LBceDice = λ1LBCE + λ2LDice (13) where λ1 and λ2 are two hyperparameters to balance each part. IV. EXPERIMENTS A. Datasets The experiments are conducted on three public benchmarks, NUAA-SIRST [8], IRSTD-1k [60], and NUST-SIRST [22], for both training and testing. NUAA-SIRST consists of 427 rep- resentative infrared images captured from various real-world scenarios, with approximately 90% of the images containing only a single target. IRSTD-1k is a more challenging dataset, including 1001 real-world infrared images with richer scenar- ios. It provides more diﬃcult cases with diverse target shapes, varying target sizes, and complex cluttered backgrounds. NUST-SIRST contains 11 real infrared sequences with a total of 2098 frames. For training, the inputs are not the raw frames but 10 000 synthetically augmented frames randomly sampled from the original sequences, while the testing set consists of 100 real-world infrared images containing diverse small targets under complex and varied backgrounds. For each dataset, we follow the oﬃcial dataset split for training and testing. Speciﬁcally, NUAA-SIRST includes 341 training images and 86 test images, while IRSTD-1k oﬀers 800 training images and 201 test images. NUST-SIRST uses the aforementioned 10 000 augmented training frames and 100 testing images. B. Processing 3College of Computer Science and Aritificial Intelligence, Fudan University Abstract Deep learning algorithms are highly data-intensive, partic- ularly for tasks requiring pixel-level annotations, such as semantic segmentation, which makes achieving pixel-level image understanding costly. Few-shot segmentation seeks to address this challenge by enabling models to segment novel objects using only a limited number of labeled support images as references. In this paper, we argue that the tradi- tional image-to-mask decoding framework places excessive reliance on the quality of the support sample, which is prone to errors when encountering class bias. Thus, we propose a novel image-to-mask denoising learning paradigm for few- shot segmentation, transforming mask decoding into a de- noising process to reduce the support reliance problem with the help of denoising diffusion models. We formulate our image-to-mask denoising learning process in two stages: an image corruption stage and a mask denoising stage. In the first stage, we introduce an adaptive image corruption method that perturbs the image based on regional seman- tics, motivated by the insight of perturbing data to pop- ulate low data density regions. In the second stage, we employ an in-model denoising paradigm, designing a net- work to facilitate support-to-query semantic propagation and mask denoising in a single forward pass. To enhance categorical discrimination for the denoising network, we incorporate discriminative attribute learning, which lever- ages base classes to train the model in distinguishing ob- ject categories and generalizing to novel classes. Extensive experiments and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating that the proposed method achieves competitive performance across various bench- marks. 1. Introduction Few-shot segmentation (FSS) [6, 19, 27] is proposed to help models adapt to novel classes with limited labeled samples on base classes. It aims to segment foreground (FG) ob- jects from the background (BG) in the query image given the mask annotations in a few support images. Comparison between (1) traditional image-to-mask de- coding, (2) noise-to-mask denoising, and (3) our image-to-mask denoising frameworks for FSS. Our method transforms mask de- coding into a composition of image corruption and mask denoising process, leveraging diffusion models to ameliorate the dependence on support samples while retaining the advantage of a prior input. FSS methods usually follow an image-to-mask decoding framework, trying to decode the mask from image embed- dings via prototype learning or pixel-level feature match- ing [10, 14, 20, 22, 30]. While being intuitive and ef- fective, these approaches expose a heavy reliance on the choice of the support example, as widely existing class bias might hinder precise semantic correspondence and lead to false segmentation results. For example, despite belonging to the same class, the support and query images often ex- hibit substantial intra-class variation, rendering the correla- tion insufficient to ensure correct matching in such support- query pairs. In contrast, objects of different classes some- times share similar appearances, colors, poses, and textures. When they simultaneously appear in the query image, this inter-class similarity can lead to incorrect pixel correlations and result in redundant segmentation. The denoising diffusion [4] probabilistic model has This ICCV paper is the Open Access version, provided by the Computer Vision Foundation. By learning the underlying data distribution, diffusion mod- els are capable of generating images that are unseen in the training set. Inspired by this idea, we try to incorporate denoising learning into FSS to overcome the instability in previous image-to-mask decoding methods. However, most existing diffusion models [9, 12, 16] are designed for the image generation task, which usually starts with a pure Gaussian noise to ensure the diversity of gen- eration, while FSS is essentially a regression task, which aims to give a deterministic prediction upon given inputs. Although an option is to condition the denoising process on those inputs, this noise-to-mask denoising approach neces- sitates careful design for feature fusion and probably has a high computational cost due to the effort in injecting the input information into the noise without prior information. Therefore, we propose an image-to-mask denoising learning framework DeFSS, which starts with a noisy im- age instead of a pure noise to leverage the denoising diffu- sion model while retaining the prior advantage in traditional image-to-mask decoding paradigms. The proposed frame- work can be decomposed into two steps: image corruption and mask denoising. We first corrupt the query image with Gaussian noise to obtain the noisy query image. Then the model learns to denoise the noisy image to the query mask. For image corruption, we design an adaptive image corrup- tion (AIC) module to corrupt the image according to a prior mask indicating the semantics of each region, motivated by the insight to perturb the data for populating low data den- sity region [17]. To get a more accurate prior mask, we propose a FG-BG-specific prior mask generator, which ad- dresses the intra-class variation issue for FG and semantic diversity issue for BG. For mask denoising, we employ an in-model denoising paradigm and design a network to de- noise the mask in a single forward pass. To address the inter-class similarity brought by blurred class boundaries, we incorporate a discriminative attribute learning (DAL) scheme to enhance the categorical discriminability of our denoising network. The proposed DAL trains the model to distinguish object categories in base classes and to gener- alize to novel classes. Unlike previous fusion-based class- specific FSS methods, our DAL decouples the label infor- mation from model inputs and avoids additional labeling on novel classes, thus aligning better with the requirement of FSS. Our contributions are summarized as below: 1. We propose a novel image-to-mask denoising learning framework for FSS by formulating FSS as a composition of image corruption and mask denoising process, which provides a new perspective for the research community. 2. We propose an adaptive image corruption method and a FG-BG-specific prior mask generator. The corruption method can adaptively add noise to the image according to regional semantics. The prior generator addresses two specific issues in previous methods and produces a more accurate prior masks. 3. We introduce a discriminative attribute learning scheme to enhance the categorical discrimination for our denois- ing network by training the model in distinguishing dif- ferent categories of FG objects on base classes and gen- eralizing to novel classes. 4. We conduct extensive experiments and analyses on two challenging benchmarks: PASCAL-5i[13] and COCO- 20i[8]. The results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Through ablation studies, we verify the effectiveness of each module. 2. Related Work 2.1. Few-shot Segmentation Few-shot segmentation (FSS) [13] aims to perform pixel- wise classification on images of previously unseen cate- gories with only a few labeled images available. HSNet [7] utilizes lightweight 4D convolutions to analyze intricate feature correlation. DCAMA [14] uses foreground and background for pixel-level correlation matching and aggre- gating. HDMNet [10] decouples the self and cross-attention to reduce overfitting and uses a distillation to transfer se- mantic correlation hierarchically. SCCAN [23] designs a self-calibrated cross-attention network to deal with the mismatch and misalignment between foreground and back- ground. ABCB [30] focuses on addressing background context bias in through iterative modulation. AENet [24] presents a plug-in ambiguity elimination network to rectify the ambiguous FG features. HMNet [25] incorporates a hy- brid Mamba Network to tackle the support forgetting and intra-class gap issues. These image-to-mask methods usu- ally rely on the choice of the support samples and is both- ered by class bias. We propose to formulate FSS in a denois- ing paradigm, leveraging the power of denoising diffusion models to address such issue. 2.2. Diffusion Model and Denoising Learning DDPM [4] proposes denoising diffusion learning to en- hance the diversity of generated images by adding noise to and denoising images. DDIM [16] constructs a non- Markovian diffusion process whose sampling in reverse process can be largely faster and speeds up the diffusion model. Stable Diffusion [12] applies diffusion models in the latent space of powerful pretrained autoencoders and greatly boosts visual fidelity. DiT [9] explores a scalable class of diffusion models based on the transformer archi- tecture. Some work have explored to apply the diffusion model in downstream tasks such as FSS. DifFSS [18] uti- lizes diffusion models to generate auxiliary support images to augment the support samples. AlignDiff [11] leverages a 22233 few real samples to guide the generation and create aligned images and masks to augment the support samples. While these methods adopt the diffusion models to generate new data and augment the support samples, our work proposes an image-to-mask denoising framework to use diffusion model as the main network for mask decoding. 3. Method 3.1. Preliminaries 3.1.1. Problem Definition The objective of FSS is to segment the foreground ob- ject in a query image given a few annotated support im- ages. Two datasets Dtrain and Dtest are specified with the base classes Ctrain and novel classes Ctest ensuring Ctrain ∩Ctest = ⊘. Following the episodic training man- ner, each episode comprises a support set S = (Is, M s) and a query set Q = (Iq, M q), where I and M denote the RGB image and mask. In training, the model learns to pre- dict a mask ˜ M q for the query image �IQ with (Is, M s) as references. In main- stream FSS methods, a frozen backbone is to extract the support feature F s and query feature F q from Is and Iq, and then match and decode features to the query mask. 3.1.2. Recapping Denoising Diffusion Models Denoising diffusion models consist of two phases: a for- ward process, where Gaussian noise is added to the input data over multiple steps, and a reverse process, which aims to denoise the data and recover the original sample. The forward diffusion process is defined as: xt = x0 √¯αt + ϵt √ 1 −¯αt, ϵt ∼N(0, I), (1) where x0 is the original data sample, xt is the noisy sam- ple at time step t. Overview As shown in Figure 2, our DeFSS includes an adaptive im- age corruption (AIC) module to add noise to the query im- age, and a discriminative mask denoising (DMD) process to denoise the noisy image to the query mask with support samples as conditions. In AIC, we use a FG-BG-specific prior generator (PG) to generate a prior mask. Then we modulate a Gaussian noise with the prior mask and use it to corrupt the image. The corrupted image is then encoded and denoised in the latent space. In DMD, a denoising network is constructed to build hierarchical conditions and denoise the embedding in an in-model manner [28]. The network output is then decoded to the query mask. We additionally incorporate discriminative attribute learning (DAL) to en- hance the discriminability of the network. A set of label surrogates are employed to represent the base classes. An inserted class token z is used to extract categorical features, and jointly optimized with the surrogates to train the net- work in distinguishing object categories on base classes. 3.3. Adaptive Image Corruption Different from the generation task, where the model usually takes in a pure Gaussian noise to ensure the diversity of generation, FSS is essentially a regression task, aiming for a precise prediction upon a given input. Therefore, it is more sensible to start with a mix of noise and input. According to the definition of the forward process in Section 3.1.2, a naive approach to corrupt the query image x0 is through a linear combination with a pure Gaussian noise as in Equation 1, which treats all pixels in the query image equally. However, since the goal of FSS is to seg- ment the FG object, the FG region should be less corrupted to maintain the semantics of the target, and the BG region should be more corrupted to reduce potential disturbance. Driven by this motivation, we aim to obtain a prior mask to indicate the FG likelihood, and adaptively corrupt the query image according to it. 3.3.1. Discriminative Mask Denoising After obtaining the noisy image by adaptive image corrup- tion, we aim to generate the query mask by a mask denois- ing process. Following [28], we formulate our denoising learning as an in-model form, i.e. we use a whole network to complete denoising in a single forward pass rather than iteratively. There are three reasons for doing so: (1) FSS is a deterministic process and does not need noise sam- pling in each reverse step (See Equation 2); (2) Accord- ing to [28], in-model denoising method is advantageous in terms of speed and efficiency; (3) The in-model framework is more like a regression task and allows us to apply existing training paradigm without modification. 3.4.1. Enhancing Discrimination for Denoising Model By learning the distribution of the FG class, the proposed denoising learning method overcomes the intra-class vari- ation and has better stability than previous matching-based approaches. However, this may introduce a blurred bound- ary across object classes, and leave the model suscep- tible to the inter-class similarity issue. Previous meth- ods [21, 26, 29] address this class bias by fusing the visual features with class label or text prompt, which requires la- beling on both base and novel classes. Instead, to align with the goal of FSS, we try to avoid the access for additional annotations on novel classes, only using the label on base classes to teach the model to learn to discriminate between different classes of objects rather than augment the data. However, directly applying the classification learning framework with one-hot labels tends to result in severe over- fitting in few-shot scenarios because the one-hot label maps an image into a single visual concept from a predefined set of categories, making the model easily overfit to base classes. Therefore, we adopt a learnable high-dimension label surrogate as the class descriptor. By generalizing fixed category-level labels to learnable attribute-level super- visions, the surrogate can well adapt to novel classes and better suit the FSS task. Accordingly, we employ an at- tribute learning approach rather than class learning to opti- mize the model and surrogates. Discriminative Attribute Learning. First, we insert a class token z to the denoising token sequence to extract categori- cal features from the sample, and create C label surrogates {sc}C c=1 to represent all base classes. Experiment 4.1. Datasets and Evaluation Metrics We conduct experiments on two well-adopted datasets, PASCAL-5i [13] and COCO-20i [8]. PASCAL-5i is cre- ated from the PASCAL VOC [1] with additional masks [2]. The dataset has 20 categories, evenly split into four folds {5i : i ∈{0, 1, 2, 3}}. Following the cross-validation tradi- tion, three folds are used for training and one for evaluation. COCO-20i is a more challenging FSS benchmark because it has more categories and the graphic layout is more com- plicated. It is curated from the MSCOCO [5], involving 80 categories divided into four folds {20i : i ∈{0, 1, 2, 3}}. Following [10], we randomly sample 10000 episodes from the validating set to evaluate the model with the mean Inter- section over Union (mIoU). 4.2. Implementation Details We take VGG and ResNet50 pretrained on ImageNet as backbones and freeze their weights to verify the effective- ness of our proposed method. We use l = 8 denoising blocks to construct the denoising network. Following SC- CAN [23], we use AdamW and SGD optimizers to opti- mize attention-related and other parameters, respectively. The surrogate dimension d is 512 for VGG and 1024 for ResNet50. The update momentum α for surrogates is set to 0.999. An addition of Focal loss and Dice loss is used as the segmentation loss function LSeg. The corruption timestamp τ is set to 400. All models are trained on eight NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPUs. 4.3. Results and Analyses Quantitative Results. Tables 1 and 2 demonstrate the re- sults of the baselines and our proposed DeFSS on PASCAL- 5i and COCO-20i. From the tables, we can draw following conclusions. (1) Our method consistently fulfills consid- erable improvements over the baselines and achieves new state-of-the-art. (2) DeFSS shows a greater capacity when support data are scarce. By a horizontal comparison, we can see that DeFSS achieves a larger performance gap in 1- shot learning than the 5-shot. For example, with ResNet50, DeFSS outperforms other baselines by 1.3 and 1.6 on two datasets in 1-shot learning, while 1.0 and 1.1 in 5-shot learn- ing. We attribute this to the ability of the denoising model to learn a distribution rather than point estimation, and ame- liorate the intra-class variation issue which is more severe when support samples are fewer. (3) DeFSS is more effec- tive when the image layout is complex. By a cross-table comparison, the improvements are more notable on COCO- 20i than PASCAL-5i. As illustrated in Section 4.1, COCO- 20i is more challenging due to a wider range of object cat- egories and more complicated visual compositions. Through the discriminative attribute learning scheme, our DeFSS enhances its discriminability among classes and addresses the inter-class similarity prob- lem, which helps our model better adapt to intricate data than the baselines. Qualitative Results. Figure 3 visualizes some of the segmentation results by the baseline (HDMNet) and our DeFSS. It can be observed that our method yields more pre- cise segmentation results than the baseline even with large class bias. The first and second rows symbolize the oc- currence of intra-class variation between support and query samples. Our method is competent in dealing with such sit- uations and produces a more complete segmentation. While the baseline tends to include pixels from other object classes, our method effec- tively reduces this type of mistake and rightly locates the target objects. 4.4. Ablation Studies Effectiveness of Image-to-mask Denoising Framework. I2M-Dec is the traditional FSS frame- work, which uses the query image as the prior to ensure a strong correlation between the output mask and the in- put image. {kb}/Track/YOLO-MS.pdf.text: 2132 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON COGNITIVE AND DEVELOPMENTAL SYSTEMS, VOL. 15, NO. 4, DECEMBER 2023 YOLO-MS: Multispectral Object Detection via Feature Interaction and Self-Attention Guided Fusion Yumin Xie , Langwen Zhang , Member, IEEE, Xiaoyuan Yu, and Wei Xie , Member, IEEE Abstract—Object detection is essential for an autonomous driving sensing system. Since the light condition is changed in unconstrained scenarios, the detection accuracy based on visible images can be greatly degraded. Although the detection accu- racy can be improved by fusing visible and infrared images, existing multispectral object detection (MOD) algorithms suf- fer from inadequate intermodal interaction and a lack of global dependence in the fusion approach. Thus, we propose an MOD framework called YOLO-MS by designing a feature interaction and self-attention fusion network (FISAFN) as the backbone network. Within the FISAFN, correlations between two modal- ities are extracted by the feature interaction module (FIM) for reconstructing the information components of each modality and enhancing capability of information exchange. To ﬁlter redun- dant features and enhance complementary features, long-range information dependence between two modalities are established by using a self-attention feature fusion module (SAFFM). Thus, a better information richness of the fused features can be achieved. Experimental results on the FLIR-aligned data set and the M3FD data set demonstrate that the proposed YOLO-MS performs favorably against state-of-the-art approaches, including feature- level fusion and pixel-level fusion. And further, the proposed YOLO-MS possesses good detection performance under diverse scene conditions. Index Terms—Feature interaction, multispectral features fusion, object detection, self-attention. Manuscript received 21 July 2022; revised 9 December 2022; accepted 13 January 2023. INTRODUCTION O BJECT detection is one of the key technologies for autonomous driving systems [1], and its performance is closely related to the safety of driving. Today, methods based on the visible images (RGB), perform well in exper- imental environments with constraints but are less effective when applied in real-world scenarios with variable environ- ments [2]. This is particularly true for the light factor. At night or in adverse weather conditions, the algorithm’s detec- tion effectiveness will be greatly reduced due to the lack of light and the inability of the RGB camera alone to provide sufﬁcient reliable information, which will seriously affect the system’s ability to make correct judgments. Therefore, it is a current challenge for this research to improve the robustness of the algorithm to different lighting and to improve the overall accuracy of the algorithm. The information that a single sensor can provide is rel- atively limited [3]. Therefore, more and more research is being conducted to enrich the information sources and improve the performance of algorithms by combining data from other sensors, e.g., depth cameras, infrared cameras, LIDAR, etc. Liu et al. [4] used three types of data, depth, RGB, and IR, to amplify the feature differences between real and fake faces, thereby improving the ability of face anti-spooﬁng models to combat attacks. Similarly, the idea of multisensor data fusion is also applicable to the task of object detection. Since infrared cameras [5] are able to capture thermal radiation, they can clearly show the outline of objects even in low light conditions. This makes visible images and infrared images naturally com- plementary [6]. Visible and infrared images are beginning to be widely used in research to improve the accuracy of pedestrian and vehicle detection. Despite the considerable breakthroughs in existing mul- tispectral object detection (MOD) methods, it remains a challenge to make proper and efﬁcient use of multispectral information, i.e., how to fuse it. Around this problem, some researchers have worked on image fusion, trying to make the fused image carry as much information as possible, i.e., image- level fusion; while others tend to unify the fusion process with the feature extraction process of the object detection network, i.e., feature-level fusion. The latter has gained much attention in recent years. Wagner et al. [7] were the ﬁrst to introduce the idea of multispectral features fusion into the CNN-based object detection framework by a two-branch network. Since 2379-8920 c⃝2023 IEEE. The exploration of fusion locations is now sufﬁciently advanced, but research on how to fuse is still ongoing. Some conventional approaches [8], [9], [10], [11] use sim- ple fusion methods, such as concatenation or element-wise sum, which can work in some scenarios but is less reliable. Considering the advantages of visible and infrared images, an illumination-aware weighting mechanism [12] is proposed to lift the contributions of visible and infrared subnetworks. Zhang et al. [13] introduced a Cyclic Fuse-and-Reﬁne module in the FSSD object detection framework, which improves the detection accuracy by reﬁning the fused features several times to obtain more discriminative features. The existing methods do achieve better results due to a more sophisticated fusion strategy, but there are still several shortcomings. 1) The extraction of visible and infrared features is per- formed in relative isolation using two branches, ignoring the interaction between the modalities, resulting in both not being adequately modulated. 2) The limitations of CNNs lead to a network that focuses more on local features and does not have the ability to establish long-range information associations. To address the above-mentioned problems of existing meth- ods, we design strategies for the extraction and fusion of mul- tispectral features in terms of intermodal interactions and the establishment of long-range information correlations, respec- tively. On the one hand, we break the isolation between the visible and infrared branches by designing a feature interaction module (FIM) that can be embedded in the backbone and enhance the interaction between the two modalities with the help of the shared branch inside the module. On the other hand, we design a self-attention feature fusion module (SAFFM) to guide the fusion process of visible and infrared features with reference to the self-attention mechanism [14], to ensure that the ﬁnal fused features can better characterize the com- plementary relationship between them. The two modules are uniﬁed into the backbone of YOLOv5 to obtain a completely new framework called YOLO-MS, which exploits the com- plementary information of multispectral images and is able to effectively overcome light variations to obtain higher detection accuracy. The contributions of this work are shown as follows. 1) We propose an MOD framework, called YOLO-MS, which uses the feature interaction and self-attention fusion network (FISAFN) as the backbone for extracting and fusing multispectral features. 2) In the FISAFN, an FIM is designed to enhance the interaction between multispectral features and an SAFFM is constructed to fuse multispectral features to ensure that the fusion features carry rich and nonredun- dant information. 3) We have demonstrated the usefulness of each mod- ule through ablation experiments and have illustrated through comparative experiments the superiority of YOLO-MS in improving the accuracy and robustness of object detection compared to existing state-of-the-art pixel-level fusion and feature-level fusion methods. II. RELATED WORK A. Multispectral Object Detection Methods The idea of fusing multispectral (RGB and IR) information has been introduced into object detection research in order to improve the robustness of object detection models to changes in illumination. So far, research has focused on two main direc- tions: 1) where to fuse and 2) how to fuse. The discussion on the fusion locations has been studied from the perspectives of input fusion, early fusion, middle fusion, and late fusion, respectively. Of these, input fusion can in turn be categorized as pixel-level fusion, while early fusion, middle fusion, and late fusion can be categorized as feature-level fusion along with the discussion on how to fuse. 1) Pixel-Level Fusion: Pixel-level fusion focuses on extracting complementary information from multispectral images and reconstructing the fused image, which is then used as input to the network to increase the level of information. Traditional image fusion algorithms consist of spatial domain-based approaches and transform domain-based approaches [15]. The spatial domain-based approach ﬁrst resolves the input images into small blocks or regions accord- ing to certain rules, then measures the saliency of the cor- responding regions, and ﬁnally combines the most salient regions to form a fused image [16]. In contrast, the trans- form domain-based methods ﬁrst convert the source image into a certain feature domain by multiscale geometric decom- position. And then, these perform a weighted fusion of the features of multiple input images, and ﬁnally perform an inverse transformation on the fused features to obtain the fused image [17]. With the development of deep learning, deep learning models, such as convolutional neural network (CNN) and generative adversarial network (GAN) have also been introduced into the ﬁeld of image fusion. DenseFuse [18] was the ﬁrst approach to fuse visible and infrared images using convolutional networks as a feature extraction and reconstruc- tion module. And, FusionGAN [19] was the ﬁrst model to use GAN to fuse infrared and visible images to advoid the limi- tations of manually designed features and fusion rules. Since then, studies [20], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25] on fusing mul- tispectral images using CNN have been widely investigated. However, this MOD algorithm needs to add an image fusion stage before the object detection stage, which will increase the computational overhead and make the network structure very unwieldy. 2) Feature-Level Fusion: Feature-level fusion uniﬁes the fusion step into the object detection network as an end-to-end framework that is receiving wider attention. Wagner et al. [7] were the ﬁrst to carry out research and proposed two frame- works, early fusion and late fusion. Subsequently, Liu et al. [8] additionally studied the two schemes of halfway fusion and score fusion, and concluded that the effect of halfway fusion was signiﬁcantly better than other fusion schemes. Hong et al. [26] also discussed early fusion, middle fusion, and late fusion in their study of remote sensing image clas- siﬁcation, and the results showed that middle fusion and late fusion were more effective in classiﬁcation. For the way to fuse multispectral features, simple fusion operations, such as channel concatenation, element-wise summation, or element-wise product are initially used in [8], [9], [10], [11], and [27]. These approaches have worked under certain con- ditions, but visible images and infrared images have different information contributions to improve the detection effect under different illumination conditions, and such simple fusion oper- ations cannot adaptively learn this change. In this regard, Zheng et al. [28] proposed GFD-SSD based on the SSD object detection framework by using two different gated fusion units to learn the contributions of different modal features. Zhang et al. Wu et al. [30] designed an effective plug-and-play CCR module to achieve effective information exchange and compact fusion. It is shown that the proposed CCR module can effectively improve the classiﬁcation performance of remote sensing data beyond other advanced methods. The fusion strategies proposed by the above approaches does work, but they still do not fully exploit the implied complementary information and lacks sufﬁcient interactions to model the intrinsic associations between multispectral features. B. Attention Mechanism The idea of the attention mechanism is inspired by the human visual attention mechanism and is widely used in var- ious computer vision tasks. The attention mechanism aims to ﬁnd the importance of different information, which makes it possible to select multispectral complementary features as well. A number of attention models have been developed. For example, SENet [31] explicitly modeled the interdepen- dence between feature channels, and adaptively acquired the importance of each feature map learning. SKNet [32] designed selective convolutional kernels that adaptively fuse branches with different convolutional kernel sizes based on the input information. CBAM [33] argued that for feature maps, there is a large amount of attentional information both between the channels and the spatial pixels. Therefore, by constructing a spatial attention module and a channel attention module to aggregate the attention information of space and chan- nel, respectively, more comprehensive and reliable attention information can be obtained. Nevertheless, the existing attention mechanisms are all based on CNN. Since convolutional operations can only pro- cess local information, the only way to capture long-range dependencies is to continuously increase the depth of the network, which can inevitably increase the cost of com- putation. Referring to the self-attention mechanism in the ﬁeld of natural language processing (NLP), Wang et al. [14] introduced this idea into the visual ﬁeld by proposing a non- local module, so that it has the ability to capture long-range dependence between pixels. However, due to the large com- putational overhead of the nonlocal module, schemes, such as CCNet [34], DANet [35], and PSA [36] have emerged to optimize its computational cost. In order to enhance the interaction between multispec- tral modalities and learn the long-range dependence between multispectral features, we propose an FISAFN. The FIM is designed with CSPNet [37] in the network to learn the implicit association information between the modalities and reconstruct the multispectral features. Meanwhile, the SAFFM is designed with reference to the channel attention module in PSA so that it ﬁlters homogeneous information from the multispec- tral features and enhances heterogeneous information to obtain fused features with greater information degree and improve the detection accuracy. III. PROPOSED APPROACH A number of excellent detection algorithms have emerged in the ﬁeld of object detection. For example, ORSIm [38] has been proposed to address the complex deformation behavior present in remote sensing images. It uses a spatial-frequency channel feature (SFCF), which considers rotationally invari- ant channel features constructed in the frequency domain jointly with the original spatial channel features to improve the robustness of the model against deformation. The authors also propose another framework, named Fourier-based rotation- invariant feature boosting (FRIFB) [39], which employs FourierHOG features that are robust to rotation and dis- placement deformation and can effectively solve the rotation problem for the detection of remote sensing images. All of these methods have achieved excellent results and advanced the ﬁeld of reﬁnement. Again, our work falls within the chal- lenging task of object detection, namely, light variation. As this work is applied to the detection of conventional targets, we have selected the well-performing and easily deployable method, YOLOv5, as an improvement over the mainstream methods for this type of detection task. YOLOv5 builds on the idea of using CSP structures in YOLOv4, using a CSP structure with residual modules in the backbone and a CSP structure without residual modules in the neck. This enhancement reduces computational effort while maintaining accuracy. In view of the excellent detection accuracy and speed of YOLOv5, we improved on it to obtain an MOD framework, named YOLO-MS. The dif- ferences between the two are shown in Fig. 2. As a result, YOLO-MS consists of three parts as follows. 1) Backbone, which uses the proposed FISAFN to extract and fuse multispectral features. Data Sets 1) FLIR-Aligned: The FLIR-aligned data set is derived from the FLIR data set, a free thermal sensing data set pro- vided by Teledyne FLIR for autonomous driving research. The FLIR data set provides data in both daytime and nighttime scenarios, including 10k annotated thermal images and cor- responding unannotated RGB images, which are captured by the visible camera and thermal camera installed on the vehicle while driving. This data set contains annotations for a variety of categories, including People, Bicycle, Car, Dog, and Others. To enable the data set to be used for MOD, Zhang et al. [13] removed the unaligned visible-thermal image pairs from it and retained only the three more frequent category annota- tions of People, Bicycle, and Car to obtain the FLIR-aligned data set. Finally, the FLIR-aligned data set contains a total of 5142 pairs well-aligned visible-thermal images with a resolu- tion of 640 × 512, of which 4129 pairs are used as the train set and 1013 pairs are used as the test set. It provides 4200 pairs of calibrated and aligned visible-infrared images, most of which have a high resolution of 1024 × 768. This data set covers four typical types, i.e., Daytime, Overcast, Night, and Challenge. The annotations of six categories of People, Car, Bus, Motorcycle, Truck, and Lamp are provided, which commonly occur in surveillance and autonomous driv- ing, so this data set is very suitable for research on MOD. {kb}/Track/FBRT-YOLO.pdf.text: FBRT-YOLO: Faster and Better for Real-Time Aerial Image Detection Yao Xiao, Tingfa Xu*, Yu Xin, Jianan Li∗ Beijing Institute of Technology {3220220586, ciom xtf1,3220220587,lijianan}@bit.edu.cn Abstract Embedded flight devices with visual capabilities have be- come essential for a wide range of applications. In aerial im- age detection, while many existing methods have partially ad- dressed the issue of small target detection, challenges remain in optimizing small target detection and balancing detection accuracy with efficiency. These issues are key obstacles to the advancement of real-time aerial image detection. In this pa- per, we propose a new family of real-time detectors for aerial image detection, named FBRT-YOLO, to address the imbal- ance between detection accuracy and efficiency. Our method comprises two lightweight modules: Feature Complementary Mapping Module (FCM) and Multi-Kernel Perception Unit (MKP), designed to enhance object perception for small tar- gets in aerial images. FCM focuses on alleviating the problem of information imbalance caused by the loss of small target information in deep networks. It aims to integrate spatial po- sitional information of targets more deeply into the network, better aligning with semantic information in the deeper lay- ers to improve the localization of small targets. We introduce MKP, which leverages convolutions with kernels of differ- ent sizes to enhance the relationships between targets of var- ious scales and improve the perception of targets at different scales. Extensive experimental results on three major aerial image datasets, including Visdrone, UAVDT, and AI-TOD, demonstrate that FBRT-YOLO outperforms various real-time detectors in terms of performance and speed. Code is will be avaliable at https://github.com/galaxy-oss/FCM. Introduction Recent advancements in deep neural networks have signif- icantly improved object detection in low-resolution natural images (2022; 2023). However, these methods struggle with efficiency and accuracy on high-resolution aerial images, es- pecially in resource-constrained flight equipment. Key chal- lenges include: i) detecting objects that are small or obscured by backgrounds in aerial images, and ii) balancing accuracy with real-time detection requirements on devices with lim- ited computational resources. To improve small object detection, increasing image res- olution (2017; 2020) is common but adds computational burden, hampering real-time performance. A key challenge *Corresponding authors. However, as shown in Fig. 1(a), backbone networks still struggle with integrating and preserving shallow information, leading to feature mismatch issues. To address the challenges associated with object detection in aerial images, we aim to achieve a more effective network design that meets the requirements for both accuracy and ef- ficiency in real-time aerial image analysis. In this paper, we propose a novel network that includes two lightweight mod- ules: the Feature Complementary Mapping Module (FCM) and the Multi-Kernel Perception Unit (MKP). Firstly, to al- leviate information imbalance within the backbone network and promote better integration of semantic and spatial lo- cation information, we introduce the Feature Complemen- tary Mapping Module (FCM). This facilitates the fusion of shallow spatial loca- tion information with deep semantic information, enhancing the consistency of spatial and semantic representations. This approach helps transfer shallow spatial location information to deeper layers of the network, improving feature alignment and enhancing the localization of small objects, as shown in Fig. 1(b). Secondly, due to the minimal representation of small ob- jects in aerial images, which often comprise just a few pix- els, these objects are susceptible to feature disappearance during convolutional neural network (CNN) feature extrac- tion. To fully utilize the limited feature information and en- hance the network’s perception of targets at different scales, we investigate the network’s receptive field and propose a Multi-Kernel Perception Unit (MKP). MKP consists of con- volutional kernels of different sizes and incorporates spatial point convolutions between these sizes to focus on details at various scales and highlight multi-scale feature representa- tion. We replace the final downsampling layer of the network with MKP. This approach enables multi-scale perception of targets, improving the network’s ability to capture features across different scales while further simplifying the network structure. To meet the requirements of real-time detection in aerial images, we propose FBRT-YOLO, which boasts fewer train- ing parameters and reduced computational load compared to the baseline YOLOv8 model (2023). Extensive experiments conducted on widely-used aerial image benchmarks such as VisDrone (2018), UAVDT (2018), and AI-TOD (2021) demonstrate that our FBRT-YOLO significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art YOLO series models in terms of the trade-off between computation and accuracy across various model scales. The results are displayed in Fig. 2. Our contri- butions can be summarized as follows: • We introduce a new family of real-time detectors for aerial image detection across different model scales, named FBRT-YOLO, achieving a highly balanced trade- off between accuracy and efficiency. • We propose a Feature Complementary Mapping Module (FCM) that enhances feature matching for small targets in deep networks by integrating rich semantic informa- tion with precise spatial positional information. • We introduce Multi-Kernel Perception Unit (MKP) to replace the final downsampling operation, enhancing multi-scale target perception, and simplifying the net- work for high efficiency. Related Work Real-time Object Detectors. Real-time object detectors are crucial for resource-constrained platforms, emphasiz- ing model size, memory, and computational efficiency. Cur- rently, YOLO (2016) and FCOS (2020) are mainstream frameworks for state-of-the-art real-time object detection. While existing real-time detectors have shown significant performance improvements on public benchmarks such as COCO (2014; 2024) for low-resolution natural images, their performance on high-resolution aerial images remains un- satisfactory. We introduce FBRT-YOLO, a specialized real- time object detector designed to excel in high-resolution aerial settings, demonstrating superior performance com- pared to existing models. Small Object Detection. Detecting small objects has long been challenging. Recent solutions include augment- ing small object datasets (2019) and using high-resolution images to retain detailed features. However, these methods often result in more complex models and slower detection speeds. ClusDet (2019) employs a cluster-based object scale estimation network to effectively detect small objects. DM- Net (2020a) utilizes a density map-based cropping method to leverage spatial and contextual information among ob- jects for improved detection performance. Despite their ef- fectiveness in small object detection, these methods suf- fer from long inference times and low detection efficiency. QueryDet (2022), while leveraging high-resolution features, incorporates a novel query mechanism to accelerate infer- ence speed for object detectors based on feature pyramids. CEASC (2023) introduces a context-enhanced sparse convo- lution to capture global information and enhance focal fea- tures, striking a balance between detection accuracy and ef- ficiency. These works propose lightweight decoupled heads that to some extent accelerate networks. However, achieving real-time detection remains challenging. Multi-scale Information Extraction and Representation. Small objects are often represented in feature maps by only a few pixels, necessitating multi-scale information to enhance the feature representation of these small objects. Many works have also been carried out from this aspect (2018; 2024). Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) integrates the deep features with the richest semantics information and the shal- low features with spatial location information, which alle- viates the problem of feature imbalance to a certain extent. PANet (2018) adds a bottom-up path on the basis of FPN, which promotes the propagation of bottom-layer informa- tion and enhances information exchange. In our work, we focus on inte- grating deep semantic information with shallow spatial po- sitional information in the backbone network. This integra- tion alleviates the imbalance in information extraction dur- ing feature extraction, thereby enhancing the representation of small objects. We employ multi-scale convolutional ker- nels to strengthen the feature representation of targets across various scales. Method We present the entire structure of FBRT-YOLO in Fig. 3. This includes two core lightweight modules: the Feature Complementary Mapping Module and the Multi-Kernel Per- ception Unit. FCM aims to integrate more spatial positional information into rich semantic features, enhancing the rep- resentation of small objects. MKP utilizes diverse convolu- tional kernels to capture target information across multiple scales. Additionally, for aerial image detection, we stream- line the baseline network by removing non-critical or redun- dant computations, further refining the network. Feature Complementary Mapping Module Insufficient integration of spatial positional and semantic information can lead to mismatches and misalignments in target information. To address this limitation, we propose the Feature Complementary Mapping Module. This mod- ule implicitly encodes more low-level spatial information into high-dimensional vectors, transmitting it to deeper lay- ers of the network. This enables the detector to capture stronger structural information, thereby enhancing the ex- pression of semantic information. The detailed structure of FCM is shown in Fig. 3, which utilizes a split, transforma- tion, complementary mapping strategy and feature aggrega- tion. The following is a detailed introduction to this module. Channel Split. We first split the channels of the input feature(Xinput ∈RC×H×W ) into two parts with αC chan- nels and (1 −α)C channels, where 0≤α ≤1 is the split ra- tio. The value of α is quite important in the network. As the network deepens, the branch with lower-level spatial infor- mation becomes more prominent, with increasing amounts of low-level spatial information being implicitly encoded into high-dimensional vectors. Enhancing the acquisition of low-level information at appropriate times can improve per- formance. The split stage can be formulated as: (X1, X2) = Split(Xinput), (1) where X1 ∈RαC×H×W , X2 ∈R(1−α)C×H×W . Orientation Transformation. To separately obtain spa- tial mappings of semantic and positional information, we send the obtained X1 to the branch composed of standard 3×3 convolution, more rich feature information is extracted on each channel, it is represented as XC in Fig. 3. X2 is sent to the branch composed of point-wise convolution, the point-wise convolution extracts relatively weak information, preserving a large amount of shallow spatial position infor- mation, it is represented as XS. This transformation process is represented by the formula: (XC, XS) = ϕ1(X1, X2), (2) where ϕ1 represents learning a mapping relationship be- tween spatial and semantic information, XC ∈RC×H×W contains rich channel information, XS ∈RC×H×W retains more original spatial location information. Complementary Mapping. Currently, the features we ob- tain, XC and XS, while effective, are discrete. This can lead to imprecise matching of target features. Therefore, we perform complementary mapping between them to compen- sate for their respective missing feature mappings, achieving efficient feature matching. We take XC, which has richer channel information, into channel interaction. It can assign unique weights to the important information on each chan- nel. This is then mapped to XS, which has low-level spatial location information features, for complementary feature fu- sion. This allows the information after interaction to obtain higher-level features. Similarly, XS with richer low-level spatial position information, through spatial interaction, as- signs unique weights to the important information on each position, and maps it to XC with rich channel information features, to achieve complementary integration and obtain higher-level features. This process achieves the guidance of stronger features to guide weaker ones, thereby alleviating the problem of information imbalance. Channel Interaction: First, we use a the depthwise convo- lution to perform convolution operations on each channel, cutting off the information between the channels, which is calculated as: XD i = ϕ2(ki, XC i ), (3) where ϕ2 represents the mapping of each feature layer chan- nel, ki is the i-th convolution kernel, XC i is the i-th in- put channel, XD i is the corresponding single output chan- nel. The output result after depthwise convolution is XD ∈ RC×H×W . then perform global average pooling to obtain the global information on each channel, and finally obtain the key in- formation weights through the sigmoid layer. The unique weight ω1 ∈RC×1×1 generated on the channel can be rep- resented as: ω1 = R   1 H × W H X i=0 W X j=0 XD(i, j)  , (4) where R represents an activation function. Spatial interaction: To further aggregate spatial informa- tion, we adopt a simple design, as shown in Fig. 3, which consists of a 1 × 1 spatial convolution layer, BN (2015) and sigmoid. Finally, we generate a spatial attention map, which is similar to channel interaction, and map it to the branch that go through the 3 × 3 standard convolution, making it more focused on spatial information.The spatial information weight ω2 generated can be calculated as: ω2 = R(F(XS)), (5) where F represents convolution mapping with spatial aggre- gation, ω2 ∈R1×H×W . Feature Aggregation. After obtaining the channel infor- mation weight ω1 and spatial information weight ω2, they are respectively mapped to the features containing XS and XC. Then the two branches are connected together to ob- tain the feature XF CM, which contains features with dual mappings of spatial and semantic relationships. XF CM is calculated as: XF CM = (XC ⊗ω2) ⊕(XS ⊗ω1), (6) where ⊗is element-wise multiplication. Overall, the FCM module adopts an information comple- mentary fusion method with relatively low computational resources. It propagates shallow-level spatial positional in- formation into deeper layers of the network, alleviating the loss of object spatial location information in the backbone network downsampling process. Multi-Kernel Perception Unit Small targets in aerial images are often obscured by back- ground noise, resulting in limited effective information. To fully leverage the available feature information, we employ a multi-kernel perception unit to detect targets at different scales and establish spatial relationships across these scales, thereby enhancing the feature representation of contextual and small target information. As illustrated in Fig. 3, the Multi-Kernel Perception Unit (MKP) concatenates convo- lutional kernels of various sizes sequentially, incorporating point-wise convolutions between kernels of different scales. The entire process can be mathematically represented as fol- lows: X′ = T2k+1(A(· · · A(Tk(X)) · · · )), (7) where X represents local features of the input, while X ′ rep- resents globally mapped features across multiple scales. Tk represents depthwise convolution with kernel size k. In our experiment, we set k = 3. A represents point-wise convolu- tion transformation. Targeted Reduction of Redundancy-Driven Network Design Currently, real-time detection models are primarily designed for traditional low-resolution image detection, but this does not apply well to high-resolution aerial image detection, resulting in significant structural redundancy. For spatial downsampling in feature extraction, channel expansion pre- cedes depthwise convolution sampling (2024). Post depth- wise convolution, there is interference between channels, leading to a loss of spatial information, which is disadvanta- geous for detecting aerial images in complex environments. {kb}/Track/AFSENet.pdf.text: IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON GEOSCIENCE AND REMOTE SENSING, VOL. 63, 2025 5642613 Adaptive Frequency Separation Enhancement Network for Infrared Small Target Detection Shuying Li , Zhe Liu, Wuwei Wang , Member, IEEE, and Qiang Li , Member, IEEE Abstract—Infrared small target detection (IRSTD) aims to accurately extract small targets from complex backgrounds. It plays a crucial role in applications such as military reconnais- sance and drone detection. Existing studies predominantly focus on spatial-domain feature extraction. However, they neglect to fully exploit frequency-domain information, which may con- tain critical patterns for comprehensive signal characterization. Consequently, this limitation results in suboptimal detection accuracy. To eﬀectively capture the structural characteristics of small targets, frequency-domain adaptive decomposition module (FDADM) is embedded into the spatial-domain encoder of the proposed network. The proposed FDADM eﬀectively improves the accuracy of capturing target details and enhances structural feature consistency. Furthermore, considering that small targets may have blurred edges in complex backgrounds, gradient localization enhancement module (GLEM) is proposed. Gradient direction and gradient magnitude consistency functions are deﬁned to precisely characterize target edges and contours, which improves detection accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can eﬀectively extract infrared small target under complex background conditions. Index Terms—Frequency feature, gradient positioning enhancement, infrared image, small target detection. I. INTRODUCTION I NFRARED images have the unique advantage of maintain- ing clear imaging in low-light conditions and under strong sunlight. Compared with traditional visible light images, infrared images can eﬀectively penetrate obstacles such as smoke and haze. This capability provides more stable and reli- able visual information, which allows for the eﬀective capture of target features in complex environments. These character- istics make infrared small target detection (IRSTD) crucial in many application ﬁelds, with the purpose of accurately identifying small, low-contrast targets in infrared images. Digital Object Identiﬁer 10.1109/TGRS.2025.3605480 technology is widely applied in nighttime surveillance [1], aerospace imaging [2], and security patrols [3], which allows for the rapid identiﬁcation of potential threats and provides real-time feedback. Unlike conventional target detection tasks [4], [5], IRSTD faces a series of unique challenges. First, the thermal radiation of infrared small targets closely matches the background radiation. As a result, the contrast between the target and its surroundings is low, which makes it hard to distinguish them clearly. Second, infrared images are often captured from long distances or in complex environments. Background noise tends to obscure the features of the target, which signiﬁ- cantly interferes with target detection. Finally, due to varying environmental conditions, the appearance, shape, and thermal radiation characteristics of infrared small targets exhibit sig- niﬁcant changes, which increases the complexity of detection. These challenges not only increase the risk of false pos- itives and false negatives but also require algorithms with higher accuracy and stability. In addition, these algorithms must maintain eﬀective detection performance in complex and dynamic environments. IRSTD techniques are generally divided into two categories: traditional methods [6], [7], [8] and deep-learning-based meth- ods [9], [10], [11]. Traditional methods typically rely on handcrafted features, with common techniques such as ﬁltering methods [12], [13], local contrast methods [14], [15], [16], and low-rank methods [17], [18]. Although traditional meth- ods achieve certain results in simple scenarios, they usually depend on manually designed features and have several clear limitations. First, these methods [19], [20] are highly sensitive to complex backgrounds and noisy environments, which makes them susceptible to interference. This interference leads to an increased false-alarm rate and missed detection. Second, local contrast methods enhance detection performance under low- contrast conditions. Their eﬀectiveness is limited when dealing with dynamic background changes or insuﬃcient contrast between the target and the background. Furthermore, low-rank methods perform well in static backgrounds. However, their eﬀectiveness deteriorates when the background assumption is violated in complex or dynamic scenes, resulting in a signiﬁcant drop in performance. In summary, these factors limit their adaptability to diﬀerent targets and situations, which leads to suboptimal performance. Some methods start from the diﬀerence between the target and the background. For example, Ma et al. [29] design high- and low-frequency reconstruction networks based on the diﬀer- ence between the frequency characteristics of small targets and background noise. These networks enhance the target and suppress the background, enabling eﬀective extraction of sparse target features. There are also some methods that design models from the network structure. For example, Lee and Park [30] design a hybrid encoder structure for IRSTD. This structure improves detection accuracy for fuzzy and low-contrast objects by dividing the image into blocks and extracting features through hierarchical stacking. Dai et al. [31] design a local attention feature modulation module. This module embeds low-level background and detail information into high-level features to enhance the features of infrared small targets. Similar studies are [27], [28], and [53]. With the advancement of technology, multiframe information and motion features become important factors in improving the accuracy of IRSTD. On one hand, Chen et al. [50] propose the SSTNet model to address multiframe information. This model captures richer motion features through spatiotemporal modeling across multiple frames, which signiﬁcantly improves detection accuracy. On the other hand, to enhance the use of motion features, Chen et al. [51] introduce the motion prior knowledge learning (MoPKL) framework. This framework innovatively incorporates motion priors into the detection process and eﬀectively guides the visual pathway to learn motion features, further boosting detection performance. A review of existing approaches shows that several challenges in the IRSTD ﬁeld remain unaddressed. To begin with, the infrared small target usually occupies only a very small number of pixels in the image. Scarce feature information is further compressed or even lost during the downsampling process in convolutional neural networks. Consequently, the risk of missed detection increases signiﬁcantly. As shown in Fig. 1(a), some methods [32], [33] focus solely on the design of network depth, which overlooks the potential for missing targets in actual detection. As a result, they struggle to handle the absence of target information. In addition, frequency-domain information highlights subtle features in the image, which helps eﬀectively separate the background from the target. However, as shown in Fig. 1(a), most existing algorithms [34] concentrate on processing infrared images in the spatial domain, which results in frequency-domain infor- mation for small targets being insuﬃciently explored. IRSTD technology based on the frequency domain remains limited, and further research is needed to fully exploit frequency- domain information to improve detection performance. As shown in Fig. 1(b), our method performs feature extraction in the spatial domain. In addition, it enhances the model’s expressive power by incorporating frequency-domain infor- mation and gradient features, thereby improving detection accuracy. To address the aforementioned problems, this article pro- poses adaptive frequency separation enhancement network (AFSENet) for IRSTD. The network is divided into two key modules. One is the frequency-domain adaptive decomposition module (FDADM), which is built upon a spatial encoder and serves as the network backbone. The frequency-domain features are precisely decomposed into high-, mid-, and low- frequency components by applying an adaptive separation technique. These components are then combined with shallow, intermediate, and deep spatial features to enhance the overall feature representation of infrared small targets. This module strengthens the feature representation of infrared small tar- gets and reduces the issues of insuﬃcient deep features or target disappearance. The other is the gradient localization enhancement module (GLEM), designed to improve small target localization accuracy. This module analyzes the gradient consistency within the target region and precisely extracts gradient information from the image. This process eﬀectively identiﬁes the edge features of the target, signiﬁcantly enhanc- ing the accuracy of the model in small target localization. In conclusion, the contributions of the proposed approach can be summarized as follows. 1) To suppress background noise and improve target detection accuracy in low-contrast infrared images, we propose FDADM. This module adaptively decomposes frequency-domain features, which fully uses texture information and captures the overall structure of the image. 2) GLEM is proposed to assist the model in more accu- rately localizing targets. The module uses the gradient direction and magnitude characteristics of infrared tar- gets to generate a gradient saliency map, which enhances the edge features of the target. 3) The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model signiﬁcantly outperforms traditional methods and achieves comparable performance with recent CNN- based approaches.
