{kb}/医学/Simultaneous Tri-Modal Medical I.text: Simultaneous Tri-Modal Medical Image Fusion and Super-Resolution using Conditional Diffusion Model Yushen Xu , Xiaosong Li(B) , Yuchan Jie , and Haishu Tan Foshan University lixiaosong@buaa.edu.cn Abstract. In clinical practice, tri-modal medical image fusion, com- pared to the existing dual-modal technique, can provide a more compre- hensive view of the lesions, aiding physicians in evaluating the disease’s shape, location, and biological activity. However, due to the limitations of imaging equipment and considerations for patient safety, the qual- ity of medical images is usually limited, leading to sub-optimal fusion performance, and affecting the depth of image analysis by the physician. Thus, there is an urgent need for a technology that can both enhance im- age resolution and integrate multi-modal information. Although current image processing methods can effectively address image fusion and super- resolution individually, solving both problems synchronously remains ex- tremely challenging. In this paper, we propose TFS-Diff, a simultaneously realize tri-modal medical image fusion and super-resolution model. Spe- cially, TFS-Diff is based on the diffusion model generation of a random iterative denoising process. We also develop a simple objective function and the proposed fusion super-resolution loss, effectively evaluates the uncertainty in the fusion and ensures the stability of the optimization process. And the channel attention module is proposed to effectively in- tegrate key information from different modalities for clinical diagnosis, avoiding information loss caused by multiple image processing. Extensive experiments on public Harvard datasets show that TFS-Diff significantly surpass the existing state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative and visual evaluations. Code is available at https://github.com/XylonXu01 /TFS-Diff. Keywords: Tri-Modal Medical Image Fusion · Super-Resolution · Con- ditional Diffusion Model. 1 Introduction Multimodal medical images have become an indispensable tool in modern med- ical diagnosis and treatment planning. Computer Tomography (CT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), Positron Emission Tomography (PET), and Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) each provide unique and complementary information [1], revealing the anatomical structure, physiologi- cal function, and molecular changes in the human body, respectively. However, arXiv:2404.17357v4 [eess.IV] 15 Oct 2024 2 Y. Xu et al due to the different imaging principles underlying these imaging technologies, images produced by various sensors exhibit significant differences in information content. Although the diversity of imaging enriches the sources of information for clinical diagnosis, it also poses additional challenges for physicians in integrating multi-source image information to make accurate diagnoses [10]. Multimodal image fusion holds promise for combining information from im- ages of different modalities [14,3] to obtain a more comprehensive diagnostic view. Currently, image fusion is mainly divided into methods based on deep learning [15,34] and traditional methods [12,33]. Deep learning-based methods often use generative adversarial networks (GANs) to simulate the distribution of fused images to obtain high-quality fused images [17]. Although GAN-based methods can generate satisfactory fused images, they suffer from issues such as training instability, mode collapse and lack of interpretability. As an improve- ment, fusion methods based on Diffusion [20,7] have been proposed, which gen- erate high-quality images by simulating the diffusion process of restoring images corrupted by noise to clean images, thereby mitigating common problems like training instability and mode collapse in GANs, and their generation process is interpretable. For example, Zhao et al. [35] proposed using DDPM for fusion tasks and employing a hierarchical Bayesian method to model the subproblems of maximum likelihood estimation. However, no deep learning fusion methods for tri-modal medical images have emerged, and only a few traditional meth- ods have conducted preliminary research on this problem. For instance, Jie et al. [9] proposed a tri-modal medical image fusion based on an adaptive energy selection scheme and sparse representation, using sparse representation to fuse texture components, and adaptive energy selection scheme to fuse cartoon com- ponents. Jie et al.[8] proposed a tri-mode medical image fusion and denoising method based on BitonicX filtering. This method analyzes pixels in terms of gradient, energy, and sharpness to achieve medical image fusion and denoising. Simultaneously, in medical imaging, due to various factors such as the resolu- tion limits of imaging equipment, time constraints on image acquisition, and the radiation doses patients can tolerate, the resulting medical images often have lim- ited resolution. Despite this, there is still an urgent demand for high-resolution (HR) medical images in clinical practice [13]. Currently, deep learning methods for super-resolution can capture fine details and accurately preserve the original structure of images [31,25,23]. For example, Mao et al. proposed a decoupled con- ditional diffusion model and extended it to multi-contrast MRI super-resolution, effectively estimating the uncertainty of the restoration and ensuring a stable optimization process [16,18]. However, performing image super-resolution and image fusion in separate steps can propagate and amplify artifacts generated in the first step, thereby degrading the quality of the image. To address this issue, research has proposed end-to-end fusion and super-resolution methods for low-resolution images [29,11,28]. For instance, Xiao et al. [28] introduced a het- erogeneous knowledge distillation network that embeds multi-layer attention to emphasize the texture details of visible light images and the prominent targets of infrared images to achieve both infrared and visible light image fusion and Simultaneous Tri-Modal Medical Image Fusion and Super-Resolution 3 super-resolution simultaneously. However, this approach is only effective for the fusion of infrared and visible light images and lacks generalizability to medical images, and it cannot achieve fusion and super-resolution for three modalities. Overall, although existing methods [9,8,31] have achieved significant accom- plishments in improving image quality, enhancing feature extraction, and im- proving single-modality medical image processing, they still face challenges in several key aspects: (1) Most research focuses on processing dual-modal source images, and there is a relative lack of in-depth studies on image processing prob- lems that cover three modalities. (2) Current methods for medical image pro- cessing mostly focus on executing single tasks, lacking strategies for jointly opti- mizing fusion and super-resolution tasks. (3) Existing technologies that achieve both image fusion and super-resolution have limited generalization capabilities for tri-modal medical images. To address these challenges, we propose an innovative Tri-modal Conditional Denoising Fusion-Super Resolution Diffusion model (TFS-Diff). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to achieve tri-modal medical image fusion and super-resolution tasks synchronously in an end-to-end manner. Our work’s main contributions are threefold: 1. The TFS-Diff model synchronously implements end-to-end tri-modal image fusion and super-resolution processing, eliminating the need for manually designing complex fusion and super-resolution network architectures. This significantly simplifies the model design process. 2. We propose a feature fusion module based on a channel attention mechanism that can learn and extract shared features and modality-specific features from different modal medical images. 3. A new fusion and super-resolution loss function is proposed to retain the sharpness, texture and contrast information of the medical images into the fused result. Meanwhile, it guarantees the stability of the model training process and the high quality of the fused results. 2 Method 2.1 Overall Architecture For multimodal image fusion and super-resolution tasks, we propose TFS-Diff, a method based on a conditional denoising diffusion probability model. This method aims to generate high-resolution fused images that contain rich multi- modal information and are highly consistent with the source images. As shown in Fig. 1, TFS-Diff achieves precise tri-modal medical image fusion and its super- resolution through a forward and reverse Markov chain process. Taking the fusion of MR-T1, MR-T2, and SPECT as an example, let the low- resolution of the three images be denoted as x ∈RHW , y ∈RHW , and s ∈RHW respectively, and the high-resolution fusion result be represented as I0 ∈R3HW . The three modal images x, y, s are input into the model simultaneously, first upsampled to the target resolution through bicubic interpolation sampling of x, 4 Y. The backbone of TFS-Diff adopts the U-Net structure from SR3 [22], with z and t as inputs to ϵθ. The backbone consists of a contracting path, an expan- sive path, and a diffusion head. Parameters are initialized using the Kaiming initialization method[6]. 2.2 Tri-modal Fusion Attention (TMFA) Block During the process of tri-modal medical image fusion, different modalities pro- vide unique perspectives on anatomical structures, physiological functions, and molecular levels. Existing fusiong methods overlook the complementarity be- tween modalities and the differences in feature importance across different chan- nels. The main purpose of the TMFA Block is to extract deep feature of the concatenated multimodal images before entering the diffusion phase of the fu- sion super-resolution network. It utilizes a channel attention mechanism to learn Simultaneous Tri-Modal Medical Image Fusion and Super-Resolution 5 the importance weights of each channel, enhancing useful features and suppress- ing irrelevant information. This approach highlights the most critical information for clinical diagnosis across different modalities. As shown in Fig.1, the structure of the TMFA Block is based on the classic SE (Squeeze-and-Excitation) block, which has been customized to adapt to tri- modal image. Initially, a Global Average Pooling (GAP) layer compresses the features of the input images C = concatenate(x, y, s) to capture global context information. Subsequently, a bottleneck structure composed of two Fully Con- nected (FC) layers is introduced to learn the nonlinear relationships between channels, where the ReLU activation function is applied to the first FC layer, and the Sigmoid activation function is applied to the second FC layer, to out- put the attention weights of the channels. Finally, these attention weights are utilized to adjust the importance of each channel in the original feature image, thus accomplishing feature recalibration to obtain the feature Zc. 2.3 Fusion super-resolution joint loss function To make TFS-Diff training converge more stably, a new joint loss design is implementedLP SF , combining Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) loss. LP SF leverages the advantages of MSE loss in terms of pixel-level reconstruction accuracy, as well as the effectiveness of SSIM loss in maintaining image structural information and enhancing visual quality to optimize both the pixel accuracy and visual quality of the image simultaneously. Additionally, the SR3 model [22] was used as the baseline for super-resolution. The model was optimized using the Adam optimizer with a fixed learning rate of 1e-4 and a diffusion step count T of 4000. The model was trained for 800,000 steps on a computer equipped with four NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPUs, with a batch size set to 32. 3.2 Objective evaluation metric In this study, we evaluated the proposed model’s performance using several quan- titative metrics: Average Gradient (AG) [4], Mean Squared Error (MSE) [27], Visual Information Fidelity (VIF) [5], Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) [26], Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR)[26], Perceptual Image Quality Loss (LPIPS) [32], Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE). These metrics assess the model’s performance in various aspects: AG measures image edge and texture clarity; MSE, MAE, and RMSE gauge pixel-level accu- racy; VIF evaluates visual quality; SSIM and PSNR judge structural similarity and noise ratio, indicating image visual effects and fidelity; LPIPS assesses per- ceptual quality from a deep learning perspective. 3.3 Comparison with SOTA methods ×2 ×4 ×8 MR-T1/Gad (Bicubic) TFS-Diff (ours) CDDFuse +SR3 DDFM +SR3 BitonicX +SR3 CTSR +SR3 TGFuse +SR3 MR-T2 (Bicubic) SPECT/PET (Bicubic) Fig. 2. {kb}/医学/Nature_Multimodal generative AI.text: 888 | Nature | Vol 639 | 27 March 2025 Perspective Multimodal generative AI for medical image interpretation Vishwanatha M. Rao1,2, Michael Hla1,3, Michael Moor4,5, Subathra Adithan1,6, Stephen Kwak7, Eric J. Topol8,9 ✉ & Pranav Rajpurkar1,9 ✉ Accurately interpreting medical images and generating insightful narrative reports is indispensable for patient care but places heavy burdens on clinical experts. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), especially in an area that we refer to as multimodal generative medical image interpretation (GenMI), create opportunities to automate parts of this complex process. In this Perspective, we synthesize progress and challenges in developing AI systems for generation of medical reports from images. We focus extensively on radiology as a domain with enormous reporting needs and research efforts. In addition to analysing the strengths and applications of new models for medical report generation, we advocate for a novel paradigm to deploy GenMI in a manner that empowers clinicians and their patients. Initial research suggests that GenMI could one day match human expert performance in generating reports across disciplines, such as radiology, pathology and dermatology. However, formidable obstacles remain in validating model accuracy, ensuring transparency and eliciting nuanced impressions. If carefully implemented, GenMI could meaningfully assist clinicians in improving quality of care, enhancing medical education, reducing workloads, expanding specialty access and providing real-time expertise. Overall, we highlight opportunities alongside key challenges for developing multimodal generative AI that complements human experts for reliable medical report writing. Medical report generation involves translating visual data such as medi- cal images and video into insightful written text, and this process is indispensable for communicating findings and guiding care across sev- eral specialties. In radiology, reporting needs are rapidly rising, partly fuelled by advances in computed tomography (CT), MRI and other complex modalities that require specialized expertise to interpret1. Reports of cardiac catheterizations, echocardiograms and endoscopies are central to patient management and information from these tests often need to be integrated with findings obtained from other imag- ing modalities. For example, a comprehensive summary of a patient’s cardiac status may require accounting of information obtained from reports of cardiac angiograms, cardiac perfusion studies, cardiac MRI, echocardiograms and cardiac CT. Synthesizing substantial visual data from these procedures into coherent and concise textual summaries represents an enormous challenge2,3 and leads to an inevitable loss of information4,5. Moreover, shortages of specialists who are skilled in reporting complex modalities lead to delays in report turnaround and errors that can significantly impact patient care6,7. AI report-generation tools show promise in addressing these chal- lenges. AI could take initial reads of exams and draft preliminary reports, enabling clinicians to work through cases more quickly, improve turnaround times, expand access to specialty-level reporting and ultimately decrease stress on the healthcare system. In remote areas without specialist availability, AI tools could potentially serve as fully autonomous preliminary reads, similar to teleradiology services8. In addition to improving clinical efficiency, automated report generation could directly improve patient care. As AI models are further developed using more robust datasets, they will be able to better predict treat- ment efficacy and diseases as well as more effectively convey health information to patients. AI models are also scalable, and in the same sense that a board of radiologists would more accurately screen for diseases compared to a single one, deploying a mixture of AI models may yield greater performance improvements9. The interactive ability of modern AI algorithms also opens the doors for them to serve a broader role as an ‘AI resident’, inspired by the workflow at academic hospitals10. Outside of solely report generation, AI assistants could improve medical education by enabling com- parisons with similar images and their reports. Their ability to offer real-time assistance is also relevant for enhancing clinician and patient understanding. An AI resident could enable treating clinicians, such as general practitioners, to probe details of a report in the context of the corresponding image and develop a deeper insight. Patients could query it under supervision to quickly gain a new perspective on their condition. Algorithms could even generate grounded and interactive reports that link particular sentences and findings to relevant areas of the image. Despite their potential, most existing AI solutions focus on auto- mating singular tasks in medical imaging, such as detecting specific https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-08675-y Received: 13 January 2024 Accepted: 20 January 2025 Published online: 26 March 2025 Check for updates 1Department of Biomedical Informatics, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA. 2Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA. 3Department of Computer Science, Harvard College, Cambridge, MA, USA. 4Department of Computer Science, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA. 5Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland. 6Department of Radiodiagnosis, Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research, Puducherry, India. 7Department of Radiology, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA. 8Scripps Research, La Jolla, CA, USA. 9These authors contributed equally: Eric J. Topol, Pranav Rajpurkar. ✉e-mail: etopol@scripps.edu; pranav_rajpurkar@hms.harvard.edu Nature | Vol 639 | 27 March 2025 | 889 conditions in individual modalities. For example, algorithms can triage chest X-rays for findings such as pneumothorax11, act as computer-aided detection tools to flag possible lesions such as lung nodules in CT12 or colon polyps in colonoscopy screenings13, or localize and character- ize abnormalities in mammograms14. These all represent important but very confined applications of AI and do not account for the more holistic and integrated analysis involved in radiology and clinical imag- ing. Interpreting exams requires synthesizing findings across multi- ple imaging modalities, correlating observations with patient clinical context and communicating integrated insights through reporting15. Most current AI tools lack the breadth to ingest multimodal data, con- textualize anomalies and generate narratives summarizing impres- sions16. Therefore, their ability to substantially reduce the workload for radiologists and other imaging specialists remains limited. They are also not as effective at identifying and describing rarer conditions or emerging diseases, which could hinder their efficacy in improving patient care and educating students. There is a major opportunity for AI to take a more expansive approach to medical imaging and reporting in the form of GenMI. GenMI models will soon be able to write compelling reports across several special- ties, as visualized in Fig. 1, and future models could ingest multiple modalities and clinical data to generate even more accurate, fluent and interpretable reports. Despite the rapid development of GenMI, there is a lack of established guidelines governing their clinical integra- tion. Furthermore, whereas GenMI models can clearly reduce clinician workloads, their role in patient care and education is less intuitive and warrants further discussion. In addition to proposing a new paradigm to leverage these exciting capabilities in a clinical setting, we discuss important challenges that must be overcome to safely realize the ben- efits of generative AI in this complex domain. Generative AI for medical report generation Until recently, medical report-generation frameworks have predomi- nantly consisted of a vision encoder and a language decoder. In this framework, the encoder extracts visual information from an image into a vector representation, while the decoder takes a vector and produces a specific output, which is language in this case. For several years, studies have built on the encoder–decoder approach, innovating novel methods to better encode image data, account for external knowledge, screen for abnormalities and more. However, the emergence of foundation models—large pretrained general-purpose AI systems that include large language models (LLMs)—has revolutionized medical image interpre- tation by prompting the development of new GenMI solutions. These GenMI approaches claim to produce more accurate medical reports as well as perform several other downstream tasks and process multimodal data using the same base model. The bulk of these algorithms build upon vision–language models (VLMs), which fuse individual vision and language models together into a unified framework that can jointly encode image and text input. Figure 2 outlines the new applications for medical image interpretation unlocked by multimodal generative AI. Incorporating LLMs The advent of LLMs has significantly affected medical report generation—algorithms now incorporate GPT variants or other LLMs as their decoder instead of smaller more traditional models17–19. Many studies have made this transition to take advantage of the knowledge and reasoning abilities of LLMs, which make them stronger and more robust decoders for report generation. Nevertheless, this represents a rather confined use of LLMs that does not take advantage of prompting techniques or their unique ability to encode multimodal input when integrated in a VLM framework. Outside of serving as decoders within the encoder–decoder paradigm, LLMs have been leveraged for report quality assurance to rewrite reports and remove hallucinations, which are usually mistaken references to non-existent prior reports20,21. There has recently been a push towards more universal vision– language systems, in which GenMI models have been developed to process multimodal input and perform various medical image- interpretation tasks including report generation and visual question answering22. Several such frameworks leverage the ability of LLMs to generate reports and answer questions on different conditions and modalities without additional labelled data18,22–29. GPT-4V is a popu- lar example from OpenAI that can recognize imaging modalities and anatomical structures in some cases, generate structured reports for pathology images, and modify these reports on the basis of medical prompts. Nevertheless, preliminary findings evaluating the model’s out of the box utility for medicine have been poor, and it faces difficulties in accurately diagnosing medical conditions30–32. Although LLMs are promising for future multimodal medical report generation, they currently face several limitations that hinder their clinical utility. LLMs are liable to biases, frequent hallucinations and inaccuracies36–38, which are especially problematic in the context of medical report generation, where remaining unbiased and maintain- ing clinical accuracy is critical. Clinicians also frequently work with incomplete information, but more complex models experience higher rates of hallucination and misdiagnosis when patient information and history are lacking39. Furthermore, the majority of foundation models used for report generation have been developed for English. Except for Chinese40, limited research has been conducted for other languages. Many of these issues can be mitigated through prudent data collec- tion and further development of LLMs, and it is important to maintain human partnership when auditing LLMs that are deployed within GenMI frameworks38,41. Multimodal processing The ability to incorporate multimodal data is an exciting avenue for more accurate medical report generation; in addition to directly pro- cessing an input query alongside an image22,27, multimodal input allows for a stronger encoding of clinical context42. Whereas prior approaches for report generation have incorporated multimodal input such as prior medical history43–47, VLMs have opened the door for more effective mul- timodal processing48. For example, one GenMI approach using VLMs can integrate various input modalities by encoding a textual domain identifier token alongside the provided image24. Despite the improve- ments conferred by VLMs, current foundation models struggle in terms of performance when integrating multimodal image input compared to clinicians36. Models adapted for multimodal tasks such as Google’s Gemini and GPT-4V are especially promising in this regard and perform better on benchmarks designed for multimodal and higher-level rea- soning in areas including health and medicine49,50. The basis of improved report generation from multimodal VLMs is their ability to learn tasks using a unified text and image represen- tational space. This type of representation learning typically imple- ments a mechanism called cross-attention, in which the model learns a matrix of ‘importance scores’ for different aspects of both the image and text sequence when producing these shared representations51,52. Contrastive learning for visual and textual encoders, in which machine learning models are trained to differentiate between similar and dis- similar data by comparing groups or pairs, is key to this learning of the shared representation space and has also led to improvements in medical report generation53,54. Although there have been many studies incorporating multimodal inputs, there are far fewer that have explored multimodal outputs, where the generated report is accompanied by some form of non-textual output to improve interpretability or diversify its clinical utility. For example, one approach is able to output bounding boxes on the input image, which significantly improves its explainability55. Another study constructed a unified model that can generate text reports as well as chest X-rays from a given input26. Outside of these studies, the usage of multimodal outputs in report generation is relatively unexplored. Improving clinical accuracy Despite their capabilities, GenMI approaches still have room for improvement in terms of clinical accuracy before active deploy- ment28,30,32. We therefore outline two methods that have been successful in enhancing clinical accuracy for prior report-generation solutions: the incorporation of external knowledge and explicit disease classifica- tion. Future GenMI models could take inspiration from these methods as part of their training and inference pipeline. One study has already incorporated retrieval augmented generation—a technique that ena- bles language models to retrieve domain-specific external knowledge during generation—within such a paradigm21,56. Several approaches have attempted to incorporate external clinical knowledge at different stages of report generation. Bottom right, the advent of GenMI has opened the door for more dynamic image interpretation. New techniques will be able to account for comprehensive multimodal context, including patient history and prior charts, as well as generate annotations and labelling to improve the quality of reports. They also allow for real-time interaction and follow up with both patients and clinicians, thereby improving the interpretability of AI-generated outputs. Nature | Vol 639 | 27 March 2025 | 891 scale, memory matrices can help consolidate knowledge by storing cross-modal mapping information between the vision and language components to better align future generated reports with the provided images57,58. Other studies incorporate knowledge on clinical findings and diseases at a broader level59–67. The most common implementation is through knowledge graphs, which are a type of computational graph that consist of nodes and edges. Here nodes represent disease states or pathophysiological features and edges capture the relations between them. Information from these graphs is typically encoded with the input using some form of graph neural network, which is a deep learning architecture that is designed to process computational graphs68. The popular knowledge graph RadGraph contains more than six million entities and four million relations extracted from the MIMIC-CXR chest X-ray dataset69 and has been used frequently in report generation70,71. In addition to clinical findings, certain studies have attempted to encode contextual knowledge relevant to particular patients based on similar reports59,60,72. Although integrating external knowledge in this manner can improve clinical accuracy, the degree to which it influences the model can affect performance73. Furthermore, there appears to be a trade-off between clinical accuracy and natural language similarity22,74,75, which measures factors including fluency, word overlap, stem similarity and number of related words between the generated text and ground truth report. Nevertheless, when external knowledge is implemented well, it is pos- sible to achieve both high clinical accuracy and language similarity55,76. In addition to external knowledge, explicitly performing disease clas- sification has also been linked with improved clinical accuracy—some papers use multi-label classification as part of their training process to encourage the model to pay more attention to clinically relevant features60,77–79. Further methods more directly utilize the outputs of disease classification in generating medical reports47,80. For example, some use the outputs to augment the initial visual features sent to the decoder when generating the radiology report81,82, whereas others perform multi-label classifications in varying anatomical regions to determine contents and focus areas of the report67,83. The disease tag outputs have even been used as starting points for writing reports, where descriptors written based on individual disease tags are com- bined to form the final report76,84. GenMI beyond radiology Given the increasing prevalence of GenMI in radiological image pro- cessing, similar approaches have been introduced in other special- ties, including pathology85 and dermatology. One all-in-one toolkit for pathology image analysis can process multimodal inputs and generate multimodal outputs by incorporating a foundation model that inter- acts with several specialized models. In addition to medical report generation, it can perform tasks including outputting bounding boxes, segmentation and answering questions86. Another GenMI approach for dermatology can provide interactive assistance and generate medical reports on the basis of images taken by the user87. More broadly, large multimodal models provide a reasonable basis for medical inference across specialties, but are still limited in their depth and current accu- racy36. Other image-interpretation models have been developed for these fields that do not incorporate formal medical report generation as a downstream task88,89. Leveraging GenMI to assist clinicians and patients Deploying an AI resident Despite the promise of these new GenMI solutions, we believe that they must be implemented in an intentional and guarded manner to fully realize their benefits in a clinical setting. With this in mind, we advo- cate for the AI resident paradigm, which serves as a guide to leverage these algorithms in a manner that empowers both clinicians and their patients (Fig. 3). An AI resident would first specialize in drafting clinically accurate reports as a starting point for residents or physicians when writ- ing their reports. During development, models could be prospectively tested in a clinical setting, as introduced in X-REM28. Then the AI resident could be fine-tuned or calibrated by an actual resident at a local level, where it can learn from the corrections and additions required. Once deployed, an AI resident could help improve the quality of reports writ- ten by radiologists or other specialists, especially in situations where information about the patient obtained through notes, dialogue, or the indications section is limited. For example, when encountering cavi- ties in the lung, an AI resident could generate questions such as “Is the patient immunocompromised?” or “Does the patient have a history of tuberculosis?” that would assist a radiologist in generating differential diagnoses in the report contextualized to the particular patient. An AI resident can also benefit clinicians and their patients by taking advantage of the real-time interactive abilities of GenMI to better dis- seminate clinical findings. Clinicians who reference medical reports when treating patients, such as general practitioners, may be interested in specific findings and could query an AI resident to find regions in the image corresponding to the report and vice versa. This is often the case with surgeons, who are interested in obtaining an in-depth understanding of the anatomy of the region they would be operating upon. Alternatively, patients could interface directly with an AI resident in a controlled setting to rapidly obtain a second opinion on their case. Patients already frequently consult platforms such as Google for online health assistance90,91, and an AI resident could formalize this process in a more effective and supervised manner. This system would also enable patients to better understand their condition and have a more active role in their healthcare. For example, particular sentences and diagno- ses in generated reports could point towards specific areas within an image that they correspond with. The patient could indicate unfamiliar terms in the report and ask the AI “What should I ask my doctor in the context of this term?”. Although patients are not expected to completely understand medical images, an AI resident could help clarify areas in the image that cause concern and thereby improve patient satisfaction following doctor–patient encounters. Patients who are more actively involved with their care as a result of such a tool may experience higher treatment compliance and better health outcomes92,93. Furthermore, the interactive ability of GenMI could allow an AI resident to assist in education. The value of real-time and personal- ized feedback in medical education is well documented94–96, and an AI resident could provide such guidance for residents and medical students. For instance, students could have educational modules that draw up similar cases from their image library to help them compare and contrast, visualize the spectrum of appearances, and ultimately gain a more thorough understanding. The order of reporting could be tweaked to allow the student to report first, with the AI resident giving feedback and suggestions based on the report. An AI resident could therefore serve as an important supplement for medical education under proper supervision from an attending physician. Aligning with human preferences Human input is imperative in ensuring that an AI resident can fulfil these roles in congruence with both clinician and patient interests. To this end, collaborative efforts between clinicians and foundation models have shown promising results, and these techniques could be incorpo- rated when deploying an AI resident in the future. Studies have shown that when clinicians review and adjust AI-generated reports, the final outputs are often comparable to, or even preferred over, reports writ- ten exclusively by clinicians97,98. Reinforcement learning from human feedback99 and direct preference optimization100 represent two such techniques that have been applied for this kind of task. A recent study has built on this notion by specifically training a conversational medi- cal report-generation model so that clinicians can provide feedback and follow up questions as needed101. Another proposed working with clinicians to audit AI imaging tools by altering the attributes of input 892 | Nature | Vol 639 | 27 March 2025 Perspective images with generative AI, observing the associated differences in model predictions, and comparing these differences to salient features identified by clinicians102. This method could be applied to improve the explainability of an AI resident. Although studies have applied these alignment techniques primarily between models and clinicians, there is potential to also involve patients in this process to capture their prefer- ences. For example, reports generated specifically for patients could be adapted to contain less medical jargon and more straightforward language surrounding the patient’s condition. While GenMI will benefit from clinician input103–105, it is likely that clinicians will also be able to learn from AI via at least three pathways. First, clinicians can take advantage of the diagnostic capabilities of AI models, especially as they continue to improve in accuracy, to gain feedback on diagnostic mistakes. Models could incorporate multi- modal output to make this feedback more intuitive and informative, where explanations coupled with bounding boxes overlaid on the original image could highlight pertinent areas of the image that may have been previously glossed over. Second, the ability of models to rapidly parse images and reports will make them a valuable tool for clinicians to quickly search for similar cases and images. Third, models could prove invaluable in assisting clinicians collaboratively brain- storm during decision-making, where probing questions offered by a model could offer insights into diagnostic patterns associated with particular conditions. Challenges in realizing the benefits of GenMI Benchmarks and evaluation metrics Medical report-generation models have previously been evaluated using natural language metrics such as BLEU106, METEOR107, CIDeR108 and Rouge-L109. These measures, although effective in determining the similarity between text inputs, do not account for clinical accuracy and are not adapted to parse and discriminate terminology that is spe- cific to medicine. With this in mind, several newer metrics have been developed to better track the efficacy of medical report-generation networks110. Specifically for radiology report generation, RadGraph F1 and RadCliQ have been proposed to predict the overlap of clinical features and radiologist-determined error scores in medical reports111. RadBench was also developed as a benchmark for foundation radio­ logy models, including medical report generation among other vision– language tasks29. Although automated metrics are convenient and scalable, human evaluation is critical towards determining the direct clinical feasibility of GenMI solutions. One study has already prospectively investigated the time saved by readers when evaluating the efficacy of generat- ing radiology reports112, and others have extended their evaluation to use human expert-level feedback to differentiate their model from the baseline28,98. Nevertheless, this area is relatively unexplored, and future studies evaluating downstream clinical effects must be conducted before medical report-generation models can be safely implemented. The need for better defined metrics is especially relevant in the con- text of an AI resident, which would serve a more consequential role in patient care. After deploying an AI resident tool, it is critical to devise methods that can maintain consistent surveillance to prevent attritions in performance and minimize chances of adversarial attacks. Recent reports have already found that the performance of popular LLMs can change significantly over time113–115, and this is especially concerning for report generation where such variances can be highly consequen- tial. Strategy for developing an effective AI resident tool, which could assist clinicians in drafting reports, offering interactive clinical expertise and educating residents and medical students. To implement an AI resident, GenMI algorithms could first be evaluated on existing datasets in an automated manner, using conventional natural language similarity metrics and clinical accuracy scores. Subsequently, they could be tested prospectively on new cases in a controlled setting with close clinician supervision. Finally, when deployed in clinic, they could be continually improved through human feedback. For example, disease prediction models could be manipulated to output particular diagnoses and outcome measures, potentially leading to overprescrip- tion, insurance fraud and falsifying clinical trials116. LLMs are especially susceptible to these attacks, and, therefore, it is imperative to ensure consistent security measures and supervision when deploying them as part of an AI resident117,118. Clinician and patient over-reliance Even after deploying and surveilling an AI resident using well-defined measures, it is important to prevent clinicians from over-reliance on its outputs. For example, clinicians may be reluctant to change the text in an AI-generated report for various reasons, including ambiguity in the accountability for mistakes, confirmation bias119 and automation bias, where they rely too much on machine-automated guidance120. This reli- ance may lead to severe consequences, where clinicians overlook rare findings that models are not primed to identify. Additionally, datasets used to train report-generation models are predominantly based on data from people of European descent121, and, therefore, models may generate lower quality drafts for minority populations; this disparity could result in compromised care for underserved communities if physicians rely too much on model outputs in such cases122. Although some studies have investigated physician decision-making when using AI123,124, there is still a great need for further work studying reliance in the context of GenMI. This issue of over-reliance also extends to patients—although the AI resident can enable patients to interface directly with real-time clini- cal expertise, these interactions should be conducted in a controlled manner so that patients do not rely on an AI resident to direct their medical care. When consulting an AI resident independently, patients cannot act on a generated report unless it is approved by a medical practitioner. Therefore, clinicians could fulfill an important role in educating patients regarding proper methods to query and understand GenMI tools for their own exploration. More generally, throughout the deployment of an AI resident, it is imperative to acknowledge the limitations of AI systems, especially in areas such as direct care, which require wider context, empathy and cognition that only humans can process and provide125. An AI resident would serve to bolster clinical care and empower patients and clinicians. Biased datasets and models Deep learning models, particularly LLMs, are prone to biases that are inherent in the data on which they are trained36–39,126. This shortcom- ing can be especially problematic in an AI resident paradigm, where models can perpetuate such biases not only in generated reports, but also in areas such as medical education and clinician understanding. Additionally, subjective human feedback is a key component in improv- ing the AI resident, which in itself may cause a biased feedback loop127. Given the gravity of these consequences, it is critical to evaluate for and mitigate biases in the development and deployment of such tools. The quality, size, and balance of training data also serve an impor- tant role in determining model bias, and therefore there is a great need for more expansive and representative datasets. Currently, the majority of progress is driven by datasets such as MIMIC-CXR, which is limited to unimodal chest X-ray scans. Other datasets are imbal- anced, where outside of the general shortage of paired images and associated reports, there are far fewer scans with abnormalities com- pared to normal scans. Even in abnormal scans, the abnormalities are usually localized to small portions of the image making them difficult for models to screen for. Additionally, scans with abnormalities tend to capture more common conditions, whereas rarer diseases are sel- dom represented. This issue may limit the ability of an AI resident to identify rare diseases and generate novel and abnormal test cases for education. Some studies have attempted to mitigate data bias through specific model components47,84 as well as explicit disease tagging to account for class imbalances63,82. Others have tried to combat this issue by extend- ing available data. For example, one proposed a new longitudinal ver- sion of the MIMIC-CXR dataset to help expand the conditions it spans and provide more temporal data75. There has also been an increasing focus on generating synthetic image data26,128,129, but fewer studies focus on generating abnormal scans. Incorporating synthetic text has also been seldom explored outside of one study that generated thousands of artificially written report samples by paraphrasing existing reports with an LLM45. It is important to note that even within available datasets, class labels themselves can be noisy, especially considering intraobserver variability for clinicians and inaccuracies in labels gathered through automated mining130,131. One promising approach to circumvent noisy labels has been zero-shot learning, which is a training technique that does not require labelled training data132,133. Whereas certain medical report-generation studies have incorporated zero-shot training to some degree22,27,85, there is a need for further development in this area to create less reliance on large datasets and mitigate model biases. New modalities and specialties Despite the number of medical report-generation studies, limited work has been conducted applying GenMI to 3D imaging, including MRI and CT scans134,135. This is partly owing to the lack of large annotated datasets in this domain, outside of a few that are not released, sparse or difficult to access. As a result, several MRI report-generation studies have focused on either writing qualitative report summaries or filling in a unified template with specific information136–138. One framework developed for generalist MRI diagnosis was pretrained on an unreleased dataset consisting of many MRI–report pairs139. In addition to 3D radiology images, GenMI techniques have been applied for other specialties in a limited manner. Ophthalmology and dermatology report generation has been successful to some degree, incorporating standard techniques such as external knowledge and disease classification within their pipelines140–142. One ophthalmol- ogy study proposed a large dataset of high-quality retinal scans along with bilingual reports and detailed annotations, opening the door for more capable GenMI models in this area143. Medical report-generation approaches in these specialties will only improve with the collection of more robust datasets and further development of data-efficient algorithms. Although the inclusion of new specialties and image types would expand the capabilities of AI tools, acquiring these kinds of large-scale multimodal datasets is very expensive; well-resourced companies can afford to gather or license these proprietary datasets, but it is unlikely that these datasets will be made available publicly for free. Further- more, even after an AI resident is implemented more pervasively in various specialties, medical institutions may prioritize using it to increase patient volume as opposed to improving the quality of care provided. As a result, it is imperative to implement an AI resident in a gradual manner, potentially beginning with only one specialty such as radiology, to ensure that it is done in a manner that prioritizes value for patients and clinical care. It is also incumbent for clinicians to stand up for the primacy of the patient–doctor relationship and ensure GenMI implementations preserve patient interests144. Conclusion Automated medical report generation represents a promising area for AI to reduce clinical burden and expand access to expert-level clinical care. The advent of GenMI creates a compelling opportunity for AI to generate higher quality reports, empower both clinicians and patients by offering interactive clinical expertise and improve future clinical care by expanding educational capabilities.

Vijaya Kishore3 · Anand Nayyar4 Received: 2 April 2023 / Revised: 21 June 2023 / Accepted: 4 September 2023 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2023 Abstract Multimodal medical image fusion is the process of obtaining relevant information from medical images. In order to create a single image that is better suitable for diagnosis, mul- tiple images from various sources are combined in image fusion for medical images. Since many of the structures in medical images are rarely discernible and the merged image typically shows blurring and lags behind the accompanying data, the complexity of medi- cal images is higher. The purpose of this research is to present a novel hybrid approach based on fuzzy sets and Undecimated Discrete Wavelet Transform (UDWT) for improved visual analysis and to lessen blurring of medical images. There is no decimation stage in UDWT. It is a non-orthogonal multiresolution decomposition. In medical images, fuzzy sets are essential for reducing ambiguity. This research paper UDWT after fuzzifying the source photos. The maximum selection criterion is used to combine low-frequency sub- bands in the UDWT domain, whereas the Modified Spatial Frequency (MSF) technique is utilized to combine high-frequency subbands. The inverse UDWT creates the merged image. Several pairs of photos are used to demonstrate multimodal medical image fusion’s efficacy. The suggested algorithm has higher entropy (6.99 bits/pixel for MR-MRA), spa- tial frequency (SF) (27.95 cycles/millimeter for CT-MRI), edge-based image fusion meas- ure (QAB/F) (0.94 for MRI-PET), and standard deviation (SD) (40.24 for X-ray-VA) as compared to other existing algorithms. The experimental data enlightens that the proposed (UDWT + Fuzzy set) approach outperforms other approaches discussed in the literature. Keywords Multimodal medical image · Image fusion · UDWT · Fuzzy sets · Fused image 1 Introduction Digital image processing systems are now possible due to advances in uses in the military, medicine, and remote sensing [1] in addition to machine vision. These methods increased data availability. In order to limit data growth and extract useful information from the source images, image fusion is employed. Image fusion creates images that are more machine- and human-friendly. With image fusion, many perspectives on a scene are com- bined into one comprehensive image. The composite image provides more accurate and dependable scene information than the original photographs alone. Combining redundant and complementary data improves multimodal medical pictures’ accuracy and uncertainty. The decision to use the insightful data from particular images is made constantly. Combining medical pictures from several imaging modalities, such as X-rays, CT scans [2], MRI scans [3], MRA scans, and PET scans [4], is a common practice in modern medi- cine thanks to image processing techniques like image fusion. Medical data processing and analysis research has grown in the recent decade. MRI can show healthy and abnormal soft tissues, while CT can better show dense structures like implants and bones. Combining CT with MRI provides a wealth of diagnostic information. Algorithm development has accel- erated signal and image processing methods by enabling picture detail extraction [5]. Com- puter-aided diagnostic systems aim for early diagnosis, sickness monitoring, and improved therapy [6]. Merging medical imaging data improves analysis. One composite image from numerous medical photos may improve analysis and diagnosis [7]. CT-MRI [2, 8–10], CT-SPECT [11], PET-CT [12], MRI-PET [13], MRI-CT-PET [14], MRI-SPECT [15], and ultrasound-x-rays [16, 17] are merged to extract clinical data. Therefore, a method called multimodal medical image fusion is required to bring together all of the necessary information. Doctors can spot anomalies using this knowledge. Medi- cal image fusion simplifies disease diagnosis. Combining multimodal images in order to extract the most data is the aim of medical image processing research. The pixel averag- ing approach [18, 19], pyramid based methods [20–23], principal component analysis (PCA) [24], hue saturation intensity (HSI) [25], discrete sine and cosine transforms (DCT) [26–28], DWT methods [29–32], ripplet transform [33], shearlet transform [34], curvelet and contourlet transform methods [35–37], and structure based fusion methods [38–40] are some of the research techniques now in use. The simplest method of combining photos is averaging the pixels from the two images, however doing so has disadvantages including reducing contrast. Blocking effects and unattractive edges in the combined image are the result of the lack of spatial orientation selectivity in all pyramid-based decomposition methods. The wave- let-based method of multiresolution fusion uses the discrete wavelet transform, which pro- vides frequency stability and precise temporal and frequency localization. The fundamen- tal drawback of DWT is its lack of shift invariance, which results in large fluctuations of the picture’s wavelet coefficients for even small changes in the input image. When analyz- ing medical imaging, the specific position of this information must be known and retained, and an undecimated discrete wavelet transform is utilized to do this [41, 42]. Zadeh’s [43] method for processing images to remove ambiguity and vagueness mainly relies on fuzzy set theory [44]. In the range [0, 1], where 0 indicates complete membership and 1 indicates no membership, it admits uncertainty in the shape of a membership function. Fusion plans should generally conform to the following standards: • To avoid distracting or confusing a human observer for further processing tasks, the image fusion approach should be reliable, resilient, and reduce noise and irrelevant ele- ments of the image. • The most crucial features of the original photos should be extracted and seamlessly integrated into the resulting fused image. ABSTRACT Glioma is a kind of brain disease with high incidence, high recurrence rate, high mortality, and low cure rate. To obtain accurate diagnosis results of brain glioma, doctors need to manually compare the imaging results of different modalities many times, which will increase the diagnosis time and reduce the diagnostic efficiency. Image fusion technology has been widely used in recent years to obtain information on multimodal medical images. This paper proposes a novel image fusion framework, target information enhanced image fusion network (TIEF), using cross-modal learning and information enhancement techniques. The framework consists of a multi-sequence feature extraction block, a feature selection block, and a fusion block. The multi-sequence feature extraction block consists of multiple sobel dense conv leaky ReLu block (SDCL-block). SDCL-block mainly realizes the extraction of edge features, shallow features, and deep features. The feature selection block identifies the feature channels with rich texture information and strong discrimination ability through the effective combination of global information entropy criterion and feature jump connection. The feature fusion block mainly comprises multi-head and spatial attention mechanisms, which can realize the fusion of intra-modality and inter-modality features. On this basis, considering the influence of tumor spatial location and structure information on the fusion results, a loss function is designed, which is a weighted combination of texture loss, structure loss, and saliency loss so that texture information from multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MMRI) and saliency information from different anatomical structures of the brain can be fused at the same time to improve the expression ability of features. In this paper, the TIEF algorithm is trained and validated on the MMRI and (Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography-MRI) SPECT-MRI datasets of glioma and generalized on the (Computed Tomography-MRI) CT-MRI dataset of meningioma to verify the performance of the TIEF algorithm. In the image fusion task, quantitative results showed that TIEF exhibited optimal or suboptimal performance in information entropy, spatial frequency, and average gradient metrics. Qualitative results indicate that the fused images can highlight tumor and edematous features. A downstream image segmentation task was used for evaluation to further verify TIEF’s effectiveness. TIEF achieved the best results in both (Dice similarity coefficient) Dice and (Hausdorff distance 95%) HD95 segmentation metrics. In the generalization task, quantitative results indicated that TIEF obtained more information in the meningioma dataset. In conclusion, TIEF can effectively achieve cross-domain information acquisition and fusion and has robustness and generalization ability. Cancer arises from the mutation or change of cellular function [2], resulting in an inability of cells to undergo programmed death [3]. These tumors affect various organs and tissues [4], [5]. While brain tumors rarely spread to other parts of the body, they remain perilous. The growth of tumors can lead to the proliferation and harm of brain tissue in neighboring areas. Even benign tumors can exert significant pressure on brain tissue, causing high-impact complications [6], [7]. Brain tumors account for about 2.17% of all cancer-related deaths, and their 5-year survival rate is only 5.6% [8]. In diagnosing brain tumors, clinicians need to combine different sequences of multimodal MRI, or CT and MRI, to determine the condition of brain tumors and further determine whether the brain tumors are benign or malignant and what kind of treatment plan to use. MMRI represents different sequences of MRI. Different MRI sequences offer distinct different details about brain tissues and anatomical features. Clinicians will combine multiple modes of MMRI to comprehensively judge the situation of tumors. In recent years, MMRI has emerged as an indispensable tool for precise and personalized medical care [9]. Unlike techniques involving ionizing radiation, MRI remains unaffected by sampling errors and internal variations. Fig. 1 shows a panel of brain tumor images obtained through various MRI sequences. Observation of Fig. 1 reveals unique characteristics across different sequences. T1 weighted imaging sequence (T1WI) presents clear anatomical structures but fails to distinctly depict lesions. In contrast, T1 weighted enhancement scanning imaging sequence (T1Gd) highlights areas with active blood flow, a crucial criterion for accentuating tumors. T2 weighted imaging sequence (T2WI) displays relatively straightforward images aiding in overall tumor assessment. Fluid attenuated inversion recovery image sequence (FLAIR) suppressing high signals in cerebrospinal fluid, delineates peritumoral edema areas. These diverse imaging patterns capture addi- tional pathological information. Given the limitations of individual imaging modes, image fusion aims to merge multi-modal images into a unified output, amalgamating complementary information to facilitate enhanced human visual perception and automated tumor detection. Multi- modal brain MRI image fusion contributes to more precise insights into lesion shapes, organizational structures, and relative space position [10], facilitating the design of more accurate individualized treatment plans. Image fusion methods can be divided into two branches: traditional fusion framework and deep learning fusion framework. Conventional methods include multi-scale trans- form [11], sparse representation [12], spatial domain method [13], and hybrid method [14]. Traditional image fusion methods are limited by factors such as the complexity of source images, the complex design of artificial fusion rules, and the prolonged processing time [15]. Medical image fusion algorithms based on deep learning are divided into convolutional neural networks (CNN), generative adversarial networks (GAN) and Transformer. On the contrary, deep learning methods CNN [16] and GAN [17] have the advantages of detailed edge texture information, reduced computational cost, and elimination of explicit fusion rule design. However, due to the localized nature of convolution operations [18], they need help to capture comprehensive global knowledge. In addition, the Transformer model has been successful in various vision tasks [19] and applied to medical imaging. Still, the Transformer model mainly focuses on the global information within the domain and ignores the crucial cross-domain integration in the image fusion task. This approach faces challenges distinguishing between target volumes, such as enhanced tumors and background. Although the results of existing multimodal image fusion algorithms are better than those of traditional image fusion methods, many things could still be improved. Due to the lack of ground truth for medical image fusion, most methods based on deep learning achieve image fusion by designing loss functions. At present, most of the design of the loss function is limited to the global pixel information level, which is not enough to form a fused image better than the source image and limits the quality of the fused image, thereby limiting the applicability of image fusion in medical applications. Although the fusion results of some methods also contain rich texture details, they have no significant contrast and cannot clearly distinguish the target from the background. The features containing rich texture information and edge information only exist in specific feature channels. Using all the shallow features for fusion reduces the fusion effect of the model. To solve the above problems, this paper proposes a brain tumor MMRI fusion network based on feature selection and attention mechanism: TIEF. This network’s fusion image of a brain tumor contains clear brain structure and anatomical information. More importantly, it integrates the description of the edema part, enhanced tumor, and necrotic tumor core of multiple modalities, and the dis- crimination degree of each area is evident, which can provide doctors with more precise and more accurate tumor information. This work contributes significantly to multiple aspects. 1) We proposed a feature information measurement block based on information entropy, a simple yet robust tool that measures feature information effectively. This block establishes efficient skip connections between encoding and 70852 VOLUME 12, 2024 Y. Comprising a cross-modality- based token learner block, transformer block, token fusion block, and spatial attention block, this block dynamically identifies critical areas within the input multi-modality deep features, enabling spatial and cross-modal fusion. 3) We proposed a new loss function that incorporates modality and tissue weighting, utilizing the regional contrast index. This function controls the preservation degree of information from source images and focuses on regions of interest vital in various medical applications. Section III introduces an efficient method tailored to the task of multimodal MRI brain tumor fusion. Section IV delves into experimental Settings, Outlines implementation details, presents fusion experimental results, performs ablation studies and gen- eralization studies, compares efficiencies and parameters, and discusses limitations and potential future directions. Section V draws conclusions based on the findings in this paper. II. RELATED WORK In this section, the focus is on reviewing pertinent research in image fusion and vision transformer techniques. These two techniques hold considerable relevance to the method adopted in this study, and we aim to provide an overview of their significant developments. A. TRADITIONAL MEDICAL IMAGE FUSION METHOD Traditional methods for medical image fusion can be categorized into spatial domain techniques, frequency domain-based fusion, and sparse representation approaches. Jiang et al. [20] introduced and applied the linked inde- pendent component analysis method in a multi-modal MRI study of Alzheimer’s patients. The study revealed increased mean diffusivity, decreased gray matter volume, alterations in anisotropy fraction and diffusion tensor patterns in the corpus callosum and forceps, and increased anisotropy fraction and diffusion tensor pattern in the regions of the superior longitudinal fasciculus passing through the descending fibers, such as the internal capsule, corona radiata, and superior longitudinal fasciculus. Wang et al. [21] proposed a joint Laplacian pyramid method integrating multiple features to effectively transfer salient features from source images to a single fused image, improving indicators such as standard deviation (STD) by 10-15% compared to other traditional methods. Kang et al. [22] presented a novel approach utilizing group sparsity and graph positivity regularization in dictionary learning (DL-GSGR) for medical image denoising and fusion. This method demonstrated more effective feature extraction compared to standard sparse representation and multi-resolution analysis, enhancing indicators like mutual information (MI) and universal quality index (UIQI) by 5-15%. Additionally, Guo et al. [23] proposed a multi- modal image fusion framework based on two-scale image decomposition and sparse representation, overcoming the limitations of single traditional methods. This approach retained finer details and edge features, showing an average improvement of 30% in metrics like edge intensity (EN) compared to optimal strategies. Traditional multimodal medical image fusion methods combine the target task to set the fusion rules and improve the image clarity by processing the complementary infor- mation between multiple images. However, although these traditional algorithms are relatively simple, they are only applicable to specific tasks or specific datasets, have limited generalization ability, and they require more demanding feature extraction and processing, leading to slower com- putation speeds. The image fusion algorithm based on deep learning provides a promising solution to solve the limitations of traditional methods by enhancing the image fusion effect. B. DEEP LEARNING IMAGE FUSION METHOD Deep learning-based image fusion methods encompass various techniques such as CNN, GAN, and Transformer. CNN excel at processing spatial and structural information within adjacent regions of input medical images. Typically composed of convolutional, pooling, and fully connected layers, CNN extract features from source images, mapping them to final outputs. These networks define image fusion as a classification problem, utilizing CNN-based algorithms to transform images, measure activity levels, and devise fusion rules. Medical image fusion based on CNN mainly includes pixel-level fusion and feature-level fusion. Pixel-level fusion is simply a weighted average of pixel values. The fusion of feature levels mostly involves joining or adding the channels of the feature map. For instance, Vaswani et al. [24] designed an early CNN-based fusion method, integrating traditional activity level measurements with CNN-based feature extrac- tion to produce fused images via pixel-weighted averages or selected fusion strategies. Similarly, Li et al. [25] designed a multi-scale CNN framework, training the network to generate decision graphs for image fusion. Despite CNN’s ability to learn from limited medical image datasets, the challenge of overfitting persists due to the scarcity of medical image samples. CNN learn hierarchical features, enhancing image content comprehension and analysis. However, because CNN only focuses on local information, the complexity and diversity of multimodal medical image fusion limits its ability to achieve optimal results. The GAN algorithm differs significantly from CNN, employing a generator and discriminator for feature extrac- tion and optimization. In GAN, the generator produces an image, while the discriminator discerns between real and generated images. The confrontation between the generator and the discriminator optimizes the fusion effect. Liu et al. [26] proposed the fusion GAN algorithm, treating image fusion as an image generation task and utilizing the least squares GAN objective to stabilize training. While GAN-based fusion methods address some issues through adversarial confrontation, the simplicity of single-scale networks in generators may lead to information loss and excessive smoothing, causing distortions in the fused image. To address this challenge, Liang et al. [27] introduced the fusion network, incorporating lightweight transformer blocks and adversarial learning to emphasize global fusion. This model enables interaction between shallow CNN-extracted features and the transformer fusion block, refining spatial and cross-channel fusion relationships. GAN models excel in retaining the selected information from source images without requiring labeled data, delivering clear and minimally distorted images. However, due to the complexity of the GAN model, the gradient is prone to disappear. Although the generator and discriminator of GAN can realize cross-modal learning, they cannot adaptively learn complementary information and screen important information and channels. Recently, Transformer-based algorithms has received a lot of attention in the image fusion community. There are many medical image fusion frames based on Transformer that have achieved impressive performance. To extract local and global information, Du et al. For better fusion result, Du et al. introduced parallel Transformer and CNN architecture into the AE- based fusion framework, (i.e., TransMEF [31]). Furthermore, Wang et al. also injected Transformer into GAN-based fusion framework to learn the global fusion relations [32]. To reduce computational costs, Guo et al. [33] proposed a hierarchical Transformer (i.e., Swin Transformer) by adopting shifted windows to compute the representation. In their method, Swin Transformer allowed cross-window connection and limited self-attention computation to non-overlapping local windows, which achieved greater efficiency and flexibility. Motivated by [34], residual Swin Transformer (RSTB) has been proposed to extract deep feature for image restoration [35]. The image fusion method based on the Transformer ignores the cross-domain information, fails to capture the local and correlation information between different modalities, and fails to highlight the lesion in the tumor tissue area emphasized by enhanced tumor and other multimodal images. This is the key to the problem of MMRI brain tumor image fusion. III. METHODS In this section, we designed a TIEF network tailored for mining and fusing multi-modal MRI images, illustrated in Fig. 2. The aim is to preserve information from diverse sensors using various models to generate a single informative image. The main challenge is to derive a trade-off between the spatial and spectral qualities of the resulting fused image and the computing efficiency. This article proposes a fast and reliable method for medical image fusion depending on multilevel Guided edge-preserving filtering (MLGEPF) decomposition rule. First, each multimodal medical image was divided into three sublayer categories using an MLGEPF decomposition scheme: small-scale component, large-scale component and background component. Secondly, two fusion strategies— pulse-coupled neural network based on the structure tensor and maximum based—are applied to combine the three types of layers, based on the layers' various properties. The three different types of fused sublayers are combined to create the fused image at the end. A total of 40 pairs of brain images from four separate categories of medical conditions were tested in experiments. The pair of images includes various case studies including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) , TITc, single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) and positron emission tomography (PET).
