They first adjusted the distribution of red and green channels in the RGB color model to eliminate color distortion, and then stretched the dynamic range of saturation and intensity in the HSI color model to enhance the contrast. Later, Zhang et al. [30] extended the original Retinex framework by performing the bilateral filter and trilateral filter operations in CIELAB color space. Recently, some specially designed approaches for enhancing underwater images are successively emerging. Marques and Albu [31] developed a contrast-guided method, called L2UWE, for enhancing underwater images with low light by considering the local levels of contrast. However, the outcome of L2UWE may introduce some artifacts and noises, as well as the illumination improvement is not significant. In [32], Li et al. designed an adaptive framework for color and contrast enhancement, and denoising by decomposing an input image into low-frequency and high-frequency components. Zhang et al. [33] also proposed a hybrid strategy based on minimal color loss and maximum attenuation map, which can effectively adjust color, improve contrast, and enhance details. Although these UIFM-free enhancement methods can increase contrast and correct the color of underwater images, they directly adjust image pixels without considering underwater imaging principles. Therefore, the enhanced results often appear to be over-enhancement or over-saturation. 2) UIFM Based Restoration Methods: Unlike UIFM-free enhancement methods, UIFM based restoration methods usu- ally recover the degraded image by deducing key parameters with regard to the transmission map and background light using some prior knowledge. In 2010, a dark channel prior, developed by He et al. [28] became popular for outdoor image defogging. Due to the formal similarity between the outdoor foggy imaging model and the underwater imaging model, some DCP-based methods and related derivations are widely applied to underwater image restoration. For example, Drews et al. [34] believed that the severely attenuated red channel cannot provide valuable information for transmission estimation, hence they proposed an underwater dark channel prior (UDCP) along with considering green and blue com- ponents of an image to estimate the transmittance. Similarly, inspired by DCP, Galdran et al. [35] proposed a red channel prior (RCP) to estimate the depth map by inverting red, green, and blue channels. Since the variety of light conditions has a great effect on the accuracy of DCP-based methods, some other priors-based methods have also been presented for restoring underwater images, such as blurriness prior [36], underwater light attenuation prior [37], attenuation curve prior [38], color line prior [39], and haze lines prior [40]. Most of the above-mentioned methods can yield satisfactory results for specific scenes, but are less effective when these priors do not hold, especially for non-uniform illumination scenes. 3) Deep Learning-Based Methods: Recently, some stud- ies [41], [42] have verified the effectiveness of deep learning methods for improving the underwater image quality in certain scenes. In [43], Lu et al. incorporated the multiscale SSIM loss into the cycle generative adversarial network (CycleGAN) [44] to restore underwater images. Inspired by the underwater scene prior, Li et al. [45] constructed an underwater convolutional neural network (UWCNN) to generate high-quality images, and extended the light-weight UWCNN model to underwater video enhancement. Afterward, Li et al. [46] proposed an underwater transmission-based muti-color space embedding network, called Ucolor, by integrating discriminative features of different color spaces to improve the visual quality of underwater images. Since a clear image is not available in underwater real-world applications, the pairs of degraded synthetic images and clear in-air images are always used for training deep neural networks. However, up to now, the authen- ticity of the synthesized underwater images has hardly been examined, which cannot accurately represent real underwater scenes. Therefore, deep learning-based methods for enhancing and restoring underwater images are limited due to the lack of large-scale and high-quality real training data. III. {kb}/新论文/2026-11-01/Multi-task_Disentang.text: IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON GEOSCIENCE AND REMOTE SENSING, 2026 1 Multi-task Disentangling Fusion Mamba-CNN for MODIS Spectral-Temporal Unmixing with Endmember Variability Modeling Motasem Alkayid, Yimin Zhu, Naser El-Sheimy, Member, IEEE, Lincoln Linlin Xu, Member, IEEE Abstract—Spectral-temporal unmixing of MODIS time series is essential for applications such as abundance mapping and spectral library construction, yet it remains challenging due to (i) spectral-temporal information coupling in MODIS data, (ii) intra-class endmember spectral variability and inter-class signature ambiguity, and (iii) the instability of naively fusing multiple expert representations. This paper presents the Multi- task Disentangling Fusion Mamba (MDF-Mamba) to address these limitations. To resolve spectral-temporal coupling, we design a disentangling architecture that pairs per-channel spectral experts with a dedicated bidirectional state-space (Mamba) temporal branch. Convolutional modules each process a single spectral channel, while the Mamba branch encodes the cross-channel seasonal trajectory, forming a multi-branch expert ensemble with soft inter-expert reweighting based on squeeze-and-excitation. For the integration of these spectral and temporal expert outputs, we introduce mHCFusion, adapting the manifold-constrained hyper-connection framework to merge the outputs in a stable and interpretable manner. Endmember variability is addressed by extending the linear mixing model with pixel-wise learnable spectral variability weights that capture intra-class endmember variation. Finally, we design a multi-task training objective that combines supervised abundance estimation with self-supervised spectral reconstruction and endmember regularization terms on the same training data, yielding a highly efficient framework for spectral-temporal unmixing. Experiments on MODIS time series covering the Alberta and Saskatchewan provinces show that MDF-Mamba achieves the best performance on 12 of 14 evaluation metrics across both datasets (7 of 7 on Alberta; 5 of 7 on Saskatchewan), ranking second on the remaining two. Index Terms—Spectral unmixing, MODIS, state space model, Mamba, endmember variability, multi-task learning, abundance estimation, mixture of experts. I. INTRODUCTION E STIMATING sub-pixel land cover fractions from mod- erate resolution satellite data is essential for broad-scale environmental observation. The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) provides daily global coverage at 250 - 1000 m spatial resolution, producing dense spectral- temporal stacks that capture phenological dynamics across diverse biomes [1, 2]. However, at this spatial resolution, This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) under Grant RGPIN-2019-06744. Yimin Zhu, Naser El-Sheimy, and Lincoln Linlin Xu are all with the Department of Geomatics Engineering, University of Calgary, Canada (email: {yimin.zhu, elsheimy, lincoln.xu}@ucalgary.ca) (Corresponding author: Lin- coln Linlin Xu). Motasem Alkayid is with the Department of Geomatics Engineering, University of Calgary, Canada, and also with the Department of Geogra- phy, Faculty of Arts, The University of Jordan, Amman, Jordan (email: motasem.alkayid@ucalgary.ca) most pixels contain mixtures of land cover types, necessitating spectral unmixing to estimate per-pixel fractional abundances. Accurate unmixing of MODIS time series is essential for ap- plications such as crop monitoring, forest disturbance mapping, and land cover change detection across the heterogeneous landscapes of western Canada. Traditional linear spectral unmixing (LSU) methods decom- pose each pixel spectrum as a linear combination of endmember signatures. On the other hand, fully Constrained Least Squares Unmixing (FCLSU) [3] solves this analytically via constrained least squares optimization [4], but assumes fixed endmembers across the scene. Extensions such as sparse unmixing via variable splitting and augmented lagrangian (SUnSAL) [5] promote sparsity through ℓ1 regularization, while nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) variants such as Spatial Group Sparsity NMF (SGSNMF) [6] incorporate spatial group sparsity via superpixel-guided regularization. While physically interpretable and computationally efficient, these approaches suffer from two fundamental limitations when applied to dense MODIS spectral-temporal stacks. Primarily, they process all spectral-temporal bands through a single shared model, conflating the physically distinct phenological cues of each spectral channel and preventing the disentanglement of channel-specific temporal dynamics. Additionally, they assume fixed endmember signatures across the entire scene, which is unrealistic given the substantial intra-class spectral variability driven by soil moisture, topography, and seasonal phenology [7, 8]. Deep learning approaches have emerged as viable alternatives for spectral unmixing tasks, offering the ability to learn nonlinear representations directly from data. Autoencoder-based methods such as PGMSU [9] and SUnCNN [10] learn latent abundance representations through unsupervised reconstruc- tion. Transformer-based architectures including DeepTrans- HSU [11] and SRViT [12] use self-attention to capture long- range spectral dependencies. Spatial-spectral attention networks such as SSAF-Net [13] and PPM-Net [14] jointly model spatial and spectral features through dual-stream encoders. More recently, 2024 frameworks have introduced contrastive learning [15], continuous variational inference [16], and spectral variability-constrained diffusion models [17] to improve re- silience against environmental noise and label scarcity. Despite these advances, deep learning methods largely inherit the same limitations: they process the full L-band stack through shared parameters, causing cross-channel interference; most retain fixed or weakly regularized endmembers that cannot capture arXiv:2610.36750v1 [cs.CV] 27 Oct 2026 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON GEOSCIENCE AND REMOTE SENSING, 2026 2 intra-class spectral variability across the growing season; and when multi-stream features are aggregated, concatenation or pooling is used with no geometric guarantee on the stability or interpretability of the fusion. The emergence of selective state space models (SSMs), particularly the Mamba architecture [18], offers a clear alterna- tive for modeling long sequences with linear-time complexity O(T) in sequence length. This makes the SSM well suited to the temporal axis of MODIS time series, where land cover discrimination relies on the ordering of phenological transitions (green-up, peak, senescence) rather than any single date spectrum [19]. While 2024 has seen Mamba adapted for spatial-spectral hyperspectral classification [20, 21], its application to unmixing remains underexplored. Recent work has applied Mamba to hyperspectral unmixing [22], but scans the SSM over the spectral (band) dimension rather than time and does not address endmember variability. While Mamba has been applied to the temporal axis of satellite image time series for crop classification [23, 24], a dedicated temporal Mamba branch for phenology-driven unmixing remains unexplored. More broadly, no existing method (traditional, deep learning, or SSM-based) jointly resolves all three limitations under a unified physics-consistent framework. Abundance supervision alone is insufficient to uniquely constrain the endmember geometry [7]: without a complementary spectral reconstruction objective, learned endmember embeddings can satisfy the abundance loss while converging to physically meaningless signatures. These open problems directly motivate the contributions of MDF-Mamba. In this paper, we present the Multi-task Disentangling Fusion Mamba (MDF-Mamba) model, a novel architecture specifically designed for MODIS spectral-temporal unmixing. The key contributions of this work are summarized as follows: 1) We design an asymmetric disentangling architecture via a hybrid CNN-Mamba multi-branch expert ensemble that assigns spectral-spatial encoding to fixed, channel- specialized convolutional experts and temporal sequence encoding to a dedicated Mamba branch, using comple- mentary inductive biases. Unlike canonical mixture-of- experts (MoE), expert assignment is fixed by channel rather than learned via a gating network, with only the downstream combination weights learned. A cross- band input stem first learns inter-channel correlations before strided indexing splits the input into six per- channel spectral streams. Six spectral BandBranches independently process a single spectral channel each (NDVI, EVI, Red, NIR, Blue, MIR) using a dual-path 2D CNN (ElementBranchCNN, d=128) that treats the T = 23 temporal observations as input channels. Each branch runs two parallel depth-three sub-networks, a spectral path (1×1 convolutions) and a spatial path (3×3 convolutions), cross-refined via a sigmoid-gated twist gate. A seventh TemporalMambaBranch processes all 23 composites jointly as a sequence of 6-dimensional multi-spectral tokens via a bidirectional selective state space model (SSM). After cross-modal alignment, a cross-branch Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) module en- ables inter-expert communication by computing soft attention weights across the six aligned spectral streams. To couple spectral and temporal representations, each spectral stream is modulated by the temporal output via an adaptive spatial-channel phenology gate that uses depthwise 3×3 convolution and sigmoid gating to produce spatially varying injection maps, replacing scalar gates with content-dependent modulation. The six modulated streams are then hierarchically grouped by physical domain: vegetation indices (NDVI + EVI), optical reflectance (Red + NIR + Blue), and moisture (MIR), reducing the fusion input from six streams to three semantically coherent groups. 2) To integrate the three hierarchically grouped expert streams, we employ a manifold-constrained hyper- connection fusion module (mHCFusion) that operates in a dfuse=64 representation space via per-stream alignment projections, applies doubly stochastic Sinkhorn-projected mixing across the grouped streams, and produces a uni- fied feature map. A scene-adaptive Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) classification head then conditions the fused representation on global scene context. An adaptive average pooling path generates per-channel scale and shift parameters that modulate the fused features before final class projection, allowing the model to adaptively adjust abundance boundary sharpness based on overall scene composition. 3) We address endmember variability through an extended linear mixing model (ELMM) in which each of the P land cover classes maintains R learnable spectral variants. Initialization follows a two-tier purity protocol: variants are seeded from high-purity training pixels (dominant class fraction ≥0.80); for biomes where no such pixels exist, a geographic grid fallback (minimum purity ≥0.30) provides spatially representative initialization. A lightweight pixel-wise variability head produces per-pixel convex mixing coefficients over the R variants. To capture non-linear mixing effects that the base ELMM cannot represent, a cross-attention reconstruction module allows each pixel to attend to the full P·R endmember variant bank to produce an attention-based spectrum, which is blended with the ELMM reconstruction via a learnable sigmoid-gated mixing coefficient. A Laplacian spectral smoothness prior further regularizes the endmember curves to enforce physical realism. 4) We design a multi-task supervised-unsupervised learning framework with curriculum training that jointly opti- mizes supervised abundance estimation, unsupervised spectral reconstruction, per-branch regularization, spectral correlation preservation, and endmember smoothness. A dedicated curriculum learning strategy up-weights reconstruction losses during early training to stabilize the endmember dictionary before shifting optimization power toward abundance refinement, combined with cosine-annealed endmember anchoring that progressively releases the model from its initialization. Extensive experiments on MODIS time series datasets covering Alberta and Saskatchewan demonstrate that MDF- IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON GEOSCIENCE AND REMOTE SENSING, 2026 3 Mamba achieves the best performance on 12 of 14 evaluation metrics across abundance estimation (MAE, RMSE), spectral re- construction (MSE, SAD), and classification accuracy (OA, AA, Kappa), ranking second on the remaining two. This outperforms eleven established baselines, including three traditional methods (FCLSU, SGSNMF, SUnSAL) and eight deep learning methods (DeepTrans-HSU, PGMSU, PPM-Net, SSAF-Net, SUnCNN, MiSiCNet, SRViT, and UNMamba). The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on spectral unmixing, endmember variability modeling, MoE fusion, and state space models. Section III presents the proposed MDF-Mamba architecture in detail. Section IV describes the experimental setup, datasets, and quantitative results. Section V concludes the paper. II. RELATED WORK A. Linear and Deep Learning-Based Spectral Unmixing Classical spectral unmixing formulates the observed pixel spectrum y ∈RL as a linear combination of P endmember spectra collected in the matrix M ∈RL×P , weighted by their corresponding fractional abundances a ∈RP : y = Ma + n, s.t. a ⪰0, 1⊤a = 1 (1) where n denotes the additive noise. While traditional methods like FCLSU [3] solve (1) analytically, they are limited by the as- sumption that endmembers remain fixed across the entire scene. To overcome this and accommodate large spectral libraries, sparse unmixing methods such as SUnSAL [5] reformulate (1) as an ℓ1-regularized optimization problem. Solved via the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), SUnSAL explicitly promotes sparsity in the fractional abundances. Furthermore, nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF)-based approaches typically estimate endmembers and abundances jointly. Notably, SGSNMF [6] extends standard NMF by incorporating a spatial group sparsity regularizer that lever- ages superpixel segmentation to enforce local homogeneity, yielding improved spatial coherence in the abundance maps. In our baseline implementation (Section IV-E), however, the endmembers are held fixed after Vertex Component Analysis (VCA) initialization to avoid model instability on near-collinear MODIS signatures. Recent deep learning methods have shifted toward learning the unmixing function end-to-end. Early approaches employed autoencoder architectures, such as PGMSU [9], which constrain the latent space to represent abundance maps while using the decoder as a learnable endmember matrix. To better exploit spatial correlations, convolutional approaches like SUnCNN [10] and MiSiCNet [25] introduced architectures inspired by deep image priors for blind unmixing. However, be- cause standard convolutions struggle to capture global context, transformer-based methods such as DeepTrans-HSU [11] and SRViT [12] employ self-attention to capture long-range spectral dependencies. Building on this, recent dual-stream architectures like SSAF-Net [13] and PPM-Net [14] employ spatial-spectral attention networks to explicitly model the interplay between local spatial context and global spectral features. Methodological evolution in deep unmixing has increasingly focused on mitigating the reliance on labeled ground truth. Approaches now include contrastive self-supervised learn- ing [15], which learns robust representations by maximizing similarity between augmented views of the same pixel, and spectral variability-constrained diffusion models [17], which iteratively generate robust abundance priors. However, while these generative and self-supervised advances help address data scarcity, many existing architectures are not explicitly designed to disentangle the complex spectral-temporal information struc- ture inherent in broadband satellite time series. Furthermore, they often fail to exploit phenological dynamics related to spectral channels, leaving a critical gap that motivates the first contribution of this work. B. Endmember Variability Modeling The assumption of fixed endmembers fails at regional-scale studies, where intra-class spectral variation is heavily driven by soil moisture, topography, and seasonal phenology [7, 8]. Early methods addressed this variability using straightforward physical constraints. For instance, ELMM [26] allows for pixel- wise scaling of endmember spectra to account for illumination changes, while bundle-based approaches maintain extensive libraries of spectral variants for each class. More recently, the focus has shifted toward complex, data-driven modeling. Concurrent preprints such as λSplit [27] employ physics- informed deep networks to learn conditional distributions over concentrations, and BLUTH [28] utilizes hierarchical unmixing to reveal endmembers across varying levels of spectral contrast. Pushing this further, cutting-edge 2024 approaches have introduced continuous variational inference frameworks [16] and spectral variability-constrained diffusion models [17] to probabilistically handle environmental noise. However, while these generative approaches are powerful, they are highly computationally intensive. Crucially, they do not jointly couple endmember variability with multi-task sequence reconstruction under a single, unified deterministic loss. C. Mixture of Experts for Remote Sensing While standard Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures rely on learned gating functions to dynamically route input tokens to specialized sub-networks, MDF-Mamba employs a different approach. As detailed in Section III-A, our architecture utilizes a fixed, channel-determined assignment paired with learned soft reweighting. Because it lacks the dynamic routing characteristic of strict MoE frameworks, we formally define MDF-Mamba’s design as a multi-branch expert ensemble. Recent frameworks have increasingly relied on conditional routing to manage complex data structures. For example, UniRoute [29] applies conditional routing to disentangle local details from global context. In remote sensing, MixtureRS [30] applies sparse MoE layers to handle confusing land cover categories by assigning specialized experts to specific spectral- spatial patterns. Similarly, MaMOL [31] introduces a modality- aware MoE to manage missing or coupled data. However, stably fusing the outputs of these multi-stream architectures remains a challenge. To address this, the manifold- constrained hyper-connection (mHC) framework [32, 33] IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON GEOSCIENCE AND REMOTE SENSING, 2026 4 provides a principled aggregation method. It projects connection weight matrices onto the Birkhoff polytope of doubly-stochastic matrices using the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm. This constraint ensures equal total signal throughput across all streams and preserves the identity-mapping property, which is essential for stable training. Adapting this robust mHC framework to fit the asymmetric spectral-temporal structure of MDF-Mamba is the focus of Contribution 2. D. State Space Models and Mamba for Remote Sensing Temporal Sequences State Space Models (SSMs), particularly the Mamba archi- tecture, enable linear-time O(T) sequence modeling through an input-dependent selection mechanism [18]. Unlike Trans- formers that rely on quadratic self-attention (O(T 2)), Mamba recurrently updates its hidden state via: ht = eA⊙∆tht−1 + ∆tBtut (2) where the input-dependent discretization parameter ∆t dy- namically controls how much past information is retained or forgotten at each timestep. This adaptive gating mechanism maps directly onto crop phenological transitions. During early green-up transitions, the model enforces strong retention (“remember” gating) to propagate key onset signals into the peak summer growing sea- son. Conversely, during harvest or senescence phases, selective decay (“forget” gating) allows the network to reset accumulated biomass states. In contrast, standard 3D convolutions apply static kernel weights uniformly across all timesteps, inherently limiting their capacity to accommodate inter-pixel phenological heterogeneity. The asymmetry of MODIS time series, where most phe- nological information is encoded in the ordering of spectral transitions rather than the absolute reflectance values [19], further motivates SSM over convolutional architectures for temporal encoding. SSMs preserve temporal causality and are theoretically equivalent to infinite-receptive-field filters [18], whereas 3D convolutions are limited to the kernel window. In remote sensing, state space models have seen rapid adoption since 2024, particularly for high dimensional spatial spectral feature extraction in hyperspectral classification via ar- chitectures such as S2Mamba [20] and SpectralMamba [21]. For spectral unmixing specifically, UNMamba [22] applies Mamba to demonstrate competitive performance with significantly reduced computational overhead compared to transformer- based alternatives. However, UNMamba and its contemporaries apply the SSM scan over the spectral (band) dimension rather than the temporal dimension, treating each wavelength as a sequence element. Closer to our setting, recent Mamba models scan the temporal axis of satellite image time series for crop classification [23, 24], confirming the value of SSMs for phenological sequence modeling, though they target hard classification rather than sub-pixel unmixing with endmember variability. MDF-Mamba addresses this gap via a hybrid CNN-Mamba architecture that applies the SSM selectively to the temporal axis while handling spectral-spatial structure through per-channel CNN experts (Contribution 1), fused via mHCFusion (Contribution 2), as detailed in Section III.
